How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.

Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.

"The American people deserve answers," he added.

Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.

Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.

How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House

How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions

Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.

Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.

According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.

Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.

Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.

It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.

Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.

Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.

Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.

The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.

Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.

But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.

Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.

Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.

Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.

Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, the world’s largest independent nonprofit research institute dedicated to plant science is building partnership with the Rwanda Institute for Conservation Agriculture (RICA).

The development is taking shape from an already existing partnership with the Rwanda Agriculture and Animal Resource Development Board (RAB) in combating Cassava Brown Streak Disease, a major constraint to cassava production in Rwanda.

The Danforth Center intends to expand its engagement from cassava disease research into broader crop improvement, conservation agriculture and scientific workforce development.

“Well, so far, it’s really been focused on Brown Streak Disease in cassava. And so, the field trials that are going on right now, which has really solved that problem,” said Dr. Giles Oldroyd, President of Donald Danforth Plant Science Centre.

Dr. Giles Oldroyd, President of Donald Danforth Plant Science Centre

From the Headquarters of Donald Danforth Plant Science Center in Saint Louis – Missouri, Dr. Giles was accompanied by a delegation of his County, including the Mayor, yesterday.

“Looking forward,” he said, “I see huge opportunities for working here at RICA on developing conservation agriculture, expanding the focus outside of cassava to also include other crops like maize and sorghum, millets. These are all crops that we work on, as well as beans. That’s a crop that I’m excited to start working on.”

“I see an opportunity to really expand the collaboration, both with RAB and with RICA, and as part of the broader Rwandan Food Innovation Partnership.”

The Food Innovation Partnership was initiated by the Government of Rwanda to turn Rwanda into a hub for food systems innovation. RICA is a key partner and founding member of the program.

Narrowing down on the partnership with RICA for example, Dr. Giles said that his institution sees an opportunity for much more exchange with students from Rwanda and the US reciprocating field visits.

For Dr. Giles, joining the partnership and particularly seeing the opportunities offered by RICA, he said “I could see a really fantastic opportunity of expanding the work we do in sustainability and conservation agriculture to also include crops that are relevant here.”

“I think what we bring to that discussion on conservation agriculture is crop improvement,” Dr. Giles said.

A partnership built on complementary strengths

For Dr. Momar Dieng, Vice Chancellor of the Rwanda Institute for Conservation Agriculture (RICA), the emerging collaboration with the Donald Danforth Plant Science Center presents an opportunity to bring together two institutions with complementary expertise and a shared commitment to agricultural innovation.

The Danforth Center, based in St. Louis, Missouri, is internationally recognized for its research in plant science and crop improvement. RICA, meanwhile, combines agricultural education, practical research, and field-based training, with a particular focus on farming methods that improve productivity while preserving soil health and natural resources.

“What makes this partnership particularly promising is the opportunity to connect world-class scientific research with practical agricultural challenges here in Rwanda. Both institutions have expertise and capabilities that can benefit the other,” Dr. Dieng explained.

One area of potential collaboration involves developing crop varieties that are not only more productive and resistant to diseases, but also better suited to sustainable farming practices.

The guest delegation was given tour of the Institute’s demo sites

Researchers at the Danforth Center are exploring how improvements in crop varieties can complement conservation agriculture, including farming methods that protect the soil, make better use of water, and reduce dependence on chemical inputs. RICA’s fields and research facilities could provide opportunities to study how these approaches perform under local growing conditions.

Another promising area is the use of advanced imaging technologies, data analysis, and artificial intelligence to monitor crop development and understand how different varieties respond to soil conditions, farming practices, and environmental stresses.

For RICA, such collaboration could strengthen applied research while creating new opportunities for students, graduates, and faculty to participate in scientific projects addressing challenges facing African agriculture.

Dr. Dieng also emphasized the value of RICA’s distinctive educational model, which places practical experience at the heart of learning.

“Our students learn by doing. They work directly with crops, livestock, equipment, and agricultural technologies, gaining the practical experience needed to translate scientific knowledge into solutions for farmers and agribusinesses,” he said.

He noted that this combination of education, research, and practical application makes RICA a potentially valuable partner for international research institutions seeking to test and adapt innovations to African farming conditions.

“Ultimately, the measure of success will be whether we can turn scientific discoveries into better farming practices, stronger agricultural systems, and improved livelihoods for farmers,” Dr. Dieng concluded.

Cole Palmer and Morgan are Chelsea team-mates

Morgan Rogers says any suggestion Cole Palmer is not committed to England "is a lie" and "nonsense".

Rogers scored the opener in Wednesday's 2-1 Uefa Nations League win over Croatia , with Harry Kane adding a penalty on his record-breaking 126th appearance for the men's side.

But his Chelsea team-mate, and childhood friend, Palmer had been left out of the squad after boss Thomas Tuchel said he "misses too many chances to impress".

The 24-year-old Palmer, who was also not called up for the World Cup, withdrew from the previous England camp in September citing a minor injury.

Forward Rogers, also 24, was asked about the criticism of Palmer following the win at Wembley, and told BBC Radio 5 Live: "He wants to be here.

"He wanted to get called up and he wanted to come and represent his country as he always has done.

"He was in quite a low place with his injuries last year and didn't feel 100% himself on the pitch, so he wants to be here and he wants to be the best version of himself.

"But he also has to look at his body. He wants to play for 10 or 15 years, he also has to manage himself. If he has to manage himself in the short term for the greater good then he has to do that and you have to fully support it.

"It has nothing to do with England or not wanting to play with England. It's a nonsense really that people are questioning someone that wants to play for England. It's a lie.

"You see the joy and smile on his face, how much he loves the game, so I honestly don't get it and he doesn't get it."

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

A must pick or unreliable? Tuchel's Palmer dilemma

History for Kane but what would England do without him?

In the three years since his England debut, Palmer has only won 14 caps, scoring two goals - including one in the Euro 2024 final defeat by Spain - and having one assist.

That is despite scoring 50 Premier League goals with 24 assists.

He was named England's men's player of the year for the 2023-24 season after some impressive form, including his strike against Spain in the Berlin showpiece.

But Palmer has only featured in three of Tuchel's 27 games since he succeeded Gareth Southgate as manager.

Some sketchy form last season, though, meant the former Manchester City player missed out on the the summer World Cup, with England going on to finish third after losing to Argentina in the semi-final.

He was named in Tuchel's first squad after that, but withdrew despite having played in all Chelsea's league games to that point.

Tuchel said this week: "We have enough number 10s and we stick to the guys who were in the previous camp because we were happy with the two and a half weeks we had together.

"I guess everyone is desperate to play for England and Cole is no exception.

"We are speaking now about a player that is not in camp. It counts when you are in camp and I just said last time that he misses too many opportunities to impress."

But the German added: "It's not personal. We will never assume Cole is in the mindset never to come to the camp.

"Cole is always in our mindset but the competition is on."

Record-breaker Kane scores winner as England qualify for quarters

Kane's top 10 England moments - which was your favourite?

Palmer should not give up hope of getting back into Tuchel's good books.

Last October, Jude Bellingham was left out of the squad for a friendly against Wales and a World Cup qualifier against Latvia.

The Real Madrid midfielder then ended up being a key part of the England team at the World Cup, scoring seven goals.

Former Three Lions goalkeeper Paul Robinson added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "You can see what Tuchel is doing when you look at what he's done with Jude Bellingham.

"It was only 12 months or so that Bellingham was getting left out of an England squad. Call it what you want, but it was management from Tuchel to make Bellingham realise that he wasn't the lone star of this team - the team was the star.

"The team was better with Bellingham in it, playing at his highest level.

"There was a lesson in his management skills with Bellingham and I wouldn't be surprised if he's doing the same now."

Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago

When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.

Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales in November 2025 .

But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.

"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."

The BBC report from last year when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia

Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of 15 November as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.

It has officially been described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in the Welsh town during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.

Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.

"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend most days who was staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms.

"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."

Wyn Smith helped her neighbours to safety when floodwaters swamped their block of flats in Monmouth, and now she's awaiting their return as renovations near the end

"We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly."

Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home.

Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface.

"Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn.

This was how ground floor residents in Jean's Chippenham Court retirement complex found their flats after Storm Claudia

"But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather."

The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events .

Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter, with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable" .

Monmouth's main shopping street was submerged after the nearby River Monnow burst its banks as it reached record levels during Storm Claudia

Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months.

"As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70.

"When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad."

Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its £1m refurbishment in the next few weeks.

Emily Frost recalls how she had to wake her two boys in the middle of the night and evacuate their family home before it was flooded during Storm Claudia

One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year.

The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surged towards her end-of-terrace cottage.

"Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC.

"They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk. I just needed to get our boys, who were then aged three and five, and they'd be back with a raft. We didn't have time to think about it."

What was supposed to be a night of celebration for her and husband Jake's 10th wedding anniversary, turned into a nightmare.

This was what Emily Frost saw of her house, on the left of this picture, as she looked back while their family were evacuated on a life raft during Monmouth's flooding in November 2025

Emily and Jake didn't take their boys when they returned home the following day where more than a foot of water had penetrated their home.

"There was sludge and mud everywhere," she recalled.

"We didn't bring the boys home for a good while because we didn't want them seeing everything that they'd treasured had been destroyed.

"It was the toll it would take on them that worried us the most."

The Frosts lived in rental accommodation nearby for six months as they ripped out the downstairs of their home and started again.

Emily and Jake, who had also been flooded in 2020, have seen their boys "playing floods" so know their children have been "trying to process" their ordeal.

This was Emily Frost's kitchen the day after her family home was flooded for the second time in five years

"They couldn't really understand why we weren't able to go home or have their things," said Emily.

"Because it's the time of year, even now when it rains they'll ask "are we staying home, is it okay? Luckily they're resilient as kids, but you still worry. People don't recover, it's something you'll just live with."

Environmental bodies estimate about 275,000 properties in Wales are at risk of flooding with another 400,000 in Scotland, while in England about 6.3 million properties - around 11.3m people - live in flood risk areas.

An official report said the River Monnow swelled to more than six-and-a-half metres after significant rainfall locally and upstream over the Black Mountains during a week where more than half-a-dozen Met Office rain warnings were issued.

Jennifer and Alan Morgan's 18th Century cottage near the banks of the Monnow had two more doors to hang after a five-year renovation when Claudia struck and they had to start it all again.

Alan and Jennifer Morgan said they spent their life savings renovating the house Alan grew up in and has been in his family for three generations so "it means a lot to us"

"I've not slept well for a year as it's been an absolutely living nightmare," said Jennifer, 70.

"The flooding was awful and the renovation has been so stressful, it's had a huge impact on us. We're not anywhere near to going back home, we probably won't be in until next summer.

"People might think because some of the shops and businesses are open that Monmouth is back to as it was before, but that's not the case - and we're proof."

The River Monnow burst its banks and the official report into the flood said floodwater reached depths 1.5m high, almost 2.5m in some extreme cases

The official Section 19 report , external into the flooding said flood warnings - where action is required as properties are in danger of flooding - were issued for all of Monmouth hours before the floods hit.

Wales' highest state of flood alert - the "risk to life and significant disruption" severe flood warning - was issued by NRW for the northern part of Monmouth on the Friday evening.

The severe flood warning for the rest of Monmouth was issued at 03:31 on the Saturday morning - but that was more than two hours after its flood defences were breached, and after shops and homes had been flooded.

Emily had signed up to NRW's free flood alert service , external but went to bed because at midnight the rain had stopped and there was no water visible - half an hour before her young family were evacuated.

Prince William was in the Monmouth area in October, visiting communities affected by the 2025 flooding caused by extreme weather conditions and met with Natural Resources Wales, the Welsh Government and Monmouthshire County Council

"When it stopped raining everyone probably thought 'oh well this has passed and we don't need to worry'," she said.

"Then the deluge of water just appeared from nowhere. It just shows how quickly it can change."

The official report recommended a review of the timing of severe flood warnings throughout the Monnow catchment "to ensure adequate advance notice is provided for people to respond effectively".

It also called for a review on the "uptake and understanding" of the flood warning service for those who live and work near the River Monnow.

NRW said it reviews their "response, recovery and flood warning thresholds" after every serious incident to "identify lessons".

Of the one in seven properties in Wales classed as being at risk of flooding, NRW said less than a third of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.

This is how the River Monnow usually looks at Monmouth but it swelled to 18-times its normal depth in November 2025, after torrential downpours during Storm Claudia

NRW argues Wales' geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.

The official report also recommended a review into whether Monmouth town centre defences were fit for purpose.

"We're looking at our flood modelling and if there's anything else that can be done," said Sara Pearson of NRW.

"We're seeing flooding that we've never experienced before and with climate change that's set to increase. We can't prevent flooding, but we can help minimise the impact."

The Welsh government said it was spending almost £1.4m in flood risk management in Monmouthshire, including £700,000 of NRW funding for works at nearby Skenfrith.

"We have made £85m available this year to Natural Resources Wales and local authorities for flood and coastal erosion schemes across Wales," the government said in a statement.

NRW said they had done work to clear rivers while the local council insist they have more workers out clearing ditches, gullies and drains.

Storm Claudia devastated the residents of Monmouth in November 2025 when the historic market town was hit by the worst floods in living memory

"We know how serious this is and how worrying it is for people," said Catrin Maby of Monmouthshire council.

"If it was only down to drain clearance we wouldn't need to worry. We need to look at the engineered defences again, we need to look at how we manage the land, we need to allocate sufficient resources into drainage and clearing those drains."

Insurance companies in the UK paid out £565m to help homeowners recover from storms and floods in 2025 - and Emily's home is one of them with flood defence measures in place like flood gates and flood doors after advice from Flood Mary , external .

"I feel safer," added Emily. "I'll still be very apprehensive when you get the flood alert, it's whether you're gonna go back to that time or not.

"But you don't feel safe, which you should do in your own house."

The report detailed problems affecting Dr Gray's Hospital but it said management failings affected the whole region

The verdict from Scotland's healthcare watchdog on NHS Grampian could hardly have been more damning.

Major problems at Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin, but deficiencies stretching across the whole region, a failure to learn from mistakes and "recurring patterns of harm".

Thursday's report from Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS) is more evidence that frontline NHS staff feel they are carrying the can for poor leadership by highly-paid, powerful people at the top of Scotland's health boards.

Centre stage this time is chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight, who earns between £170,000 and £175,000 a year. She ordered this review, but does not escape blame.

'Dramatic action' needed after NHS Grampian leaders criticised in damning report - Swinney

The report reveals she was forced into a humiliating apology earlier this year, for giving misleading information about a review into a patient's death during surgery.

Not only did HIS find the investigation into the death was inadequate, it also found the chief executive then misled HIS by saying senior executives had not seen the review or signed it off.

In fact, executive medical director Hugh Bishop had been sent the review, and had discussed it in a meeting, but claimed he had "no recollection" of this.

Misinformation provided by Skaife-Knight to the watchdog caused "significant distress" to staff at lower levels, who felt the management had tried to shift the blame onto them.

She apologised to both HIS and the affected staff, and took steps "intended to rebuild trust".

Some of the people in senior positions at the time of the investigation. L-R: Laura Skaife-Knight, chief executive; Paul Bachoo, former acute medical director; Dr June Brown, former executive nurse director; Dr Adam Coldwells, former interim chief executive; Dr Hugh Farrow Bishop, former executive medical director

HIS has described this as the most serious review it has ever had to undertake – and it details a pattern of management failure that goes beyond a single individual.

Weak leadership across the whole of NHS Grampian led to failures in recruitment, in management, in governance.

It highlights repeated failures to act on warnings about patient safety or to learn from mistakes.

For now, the Health Secretary Angela Constance has said she is keeping faith in Skaife-Knight, saying "she has operated with candour" and "put her hands up when she made mistakes".

Tell us about your experiences of health care with NHS Grampian

Constance said almost half of the board had changed, a new chairperson was about to step in and she expected them to hold senior executives to account.

With NHS Grampian already in special measures because of financial difficulties, further escalation is inevitable.

The health secretary said she would update parliament next week on what further action the government will take.

For now it is the north east of Scotland in the spotlight, but these are themes that will resonate with NHS staff right across the country.

In July, emergency medicine consultants in Glasgow wrote to Health Improvement Scotland warning of a risk of "whole-system failure" and ongoing risks to patient safety.

Health Secretary Angela Constance will update parliament next week on what further action the government will take

The doctors said the situation in the emergency department at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital had deteriorated since an inspection in 2024.

They, too, held health board executives responsible, noting staff had scored their confidence in leadership at 32/100 in a recent survey.

They questioned the transparency of their chief executive, Prof Jann Gardner, claiming she encouraged them to engage with a 2025 independent review of culture and relationships, the results of which have never been published.

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde said it continued to address the issues raised and that a programme of improvement work was ongoing.

Elsewhere, the chief executive of NHS Ayrshire and Arran also stepped down this year, after it suffered financial near-collapse

No-one can doubt NHS bosses have a tough job but they are all paid generous six-figure salaries.

Public perception around their performance will be a talking point for the government and MSPs as they move forward with plans announced in September to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two .

There is a debate about whether this is the right move for patients, but there is also a question over whether huge structural changes can improve the accountability of NHS leadership or not.

More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests.

The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%.

Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond.

Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network.

BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted.

Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways.

They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged.

These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets.

The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours.

Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024.

More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year – an average of about 274 a day.

It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.

The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).

Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.

However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.

Scottish Water figures , external show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day.

When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day.

The Clyde Estuary also recorded the longest duration of spills - more than 25,000 hours - followed by the River Clyde with more than 15,000 hours.

Barcloy Mill Burn in Dumfries and Galloway, which is one of the newly-monitored sites, received the most spills last year, with a total of almost 3,500.

The data suggests that 225 sites recorded no spills and 525 recorded fewer than 10. There may also be errors which suggest a monitor is active when it is not.

There were 1,270 spills, totalling almost 1,500 hours, last year into West Lothian's River Almond, which is nearly 28 miles in length.

Local campaigner Ruth Plevin said swimming in the river was part of her childhood and that she now wants to protect it for her own grandchildren.

She said any investment in improving the infrastructure of the water system was welcome.

"It's what's not visible that is our concern - the microplastics, the pharmaceuticals, the agrichemicals, stuff that you can't see," she said.

Ruth Plevin wants the River Almond clean for her grandchildren

Plevin, a member of the River Almond Action Group, said she wants the group's legacy to be clean, safe water.

"It's precious and I think we need to regard it as precious. Value it, look after it and make it safe.

"I want it to be clean - it's not a lot to ask for, really," she said.

Further along the east coast at Belhaven in East Lothian, surfer Brian Allen has been testing the local water for pollution.

Each week he sends samples to an accredited laboratory to be tested for E.coli and intestinal enterococci.

He says this is the same sampling as done by Sepa, except he tests all year round and not just during the bathing season.

Sepa monitors bathing water quality at about 80 sites across Scotland between May and September. It also looks out for algae, seaweed and waste.

Brian Allen said most of Belhaven's water testing has been positive

Allen, the regional representative for Surfers Against Sewage, said the results had been providing "really good news" for Belhaven.

He said 86% of the samples were rated as excellent, good or sufficient water quality, which was fine for recreational water users.

"In fact 77% of the results are coming back as excellent. What we don't know is whether that picture is being replicated across the rest of Scotland," he said.

Allen welcomed Scottish Water's increase in data publishing and said working collaboratively would help build up a bigger picture of water quality.

He said the figures had showed there were almost daily discharges from the two overflows in the area – but it was not known if there was a link between discharges and water quality.

One of them, at West Barns at Dunbar, recorded 3,300 spills last year - the second highest number in Scotland last year and a newly-monitored site.

Simon Parsons, director for wastewater at Scottish Water, said most of the time overflows were doing the job they were designed for - draining rainwater out of the sewer system.

"The vast majority of those spills aren't harmful to the environment because they're nearly always about rainwater," he explained.

Scottish Water said 99% of spills were rainwater, surface water, road run-off, "grey" water from households (not human waste), infiltration of groundwater, and trade effluent.

The overflow monitors identified more than 100,000 spills last year

Parsons said the increase in monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network and helped identify locations requiring improvement.

"We didn't necessarily know how and when our overflows were operating so we've got a much better picture now than we've ever had before.

"We can actually identify those areas where we need to think about investment.

"We've got a number of locations across Scotland where actually we've identified links between how our pumps work and how our treatment works work, which have told us where we do get some spills when we shouldn't have them - and we'll make the improvements."

Scottish Water's Simon Parsons said the monitors help identify problems in the system

Monitoring in Scotland remains far lower than in England, which has 100% coverage .

Differences in recording means Scotland's figures are not directly comparable with the rest of the UK.

Scottish Water said its monitoring had now grown to about 50% and that it was aiming to reach 100% over the next five to six years.

Parsons said the cost was relatively small but represented good value in terms of the intelligence they provided.

Harry Kane is now England's most-capped men's player as well as his country's record goalscorer, but harder to quantify is where these achievements place him among the Three Lions' greatest ever players.

This is a tricky debate with so many variables and a timescale as old as the game itself and, to my mind, not merely a determination of a player's individual ability but also a measure of their impact upon the nation's psyche.

Ballon d'Or winners Stanley Matthews, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen would surely have a shout if the criteria was such, not to mention genius technicians such as Glenn Hoddle, Chris Waddle and John Barnes.

Likewise, if any England boss managed to extract the best from Paul Scholes, Steven Gerrard and Frank Lampard they would be surely making a classic late dart from midfield.

But to qualify as one of the greatest England players of all time, you need the above ability combined with an impactful overall contribution - those memorable moments and an element of longevity - in a Three Lions shirt.

It might be controversial then to leave out Geoff Hurst, who produced the most recognisable performance in England history, while the man he replaced, Jimmy Greaves, would be a shoo-in were it not for injury earlier in the tournament.

It is also hard to rank the contribution of those whose best football came outside of major tournaments and before the dawn of continental competitions - see Eddie Hapgood, Tom Finney, Nat Lofthouse, Dixie Dean et al.

There are only 10 spots, after all, so here we go.

Spice Boy. Celebrity. Galactico. There is no argument David Beckham is one of the most iconic England players of all time, but he backed it up on the pitch, too.

Beckham was the face of the Three Lions for a generation, and to his credit managed to overcome the vicious fallout of his red card against Argentina in 1998.

At times he seemed to single-handedly carry England, most notably scoring a 93rd-minute free-kick against Greece to qualify for the 2002 World Cup.

Beckham's former team-mate Gary Neville called him the "most influential player out of England in transforming football".

It's true. On top of 115 caps, Beckham was part of Manchester United's 1999 Treble-winning outfit - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up - before joining Real Madrid.

His profile was truly global with spells at LA Galaxy, AC Milan and Paris St-Germain.

David Beckham scored 17 goals for England, including five free-kicks

There's arguably no England star fans forged an emotional attachment with more than Gazza - crying with him in 1990, rejoicing in his spectacular effort against Scotland and desperately willing him to connect during that Euro 96 semi-final defeat by Germany.

Gascoigne won 57 caps and scored 10 goals. At his peak, he was captivating - transcending football as a cultural phenomenon during the summers of '90 and '96, having joined a star-studded Serie A between those tournaments.

Creative, unpredictable, vulnerable. He was a loveable but flawed genius.

He suffered long-term injuries, as England missed out on the World Cup in the USA, but helped the Three Lions qualify for France 98 before being dropped from the final squad, famously wrecking boss Glenn Hoddle's office.

Gascoigne, Poborsky , McCoist - Goals that defined Euro 96

Goalscorers often grab the headlines but I've tried to credit players across positions and eras. From a defensive point of view Ashley Cole, arguably England's best-ever full-back, was close to making it.

But instead it's the great Billy Wright, the first men's player to surpass a century of international caps, including a remarkable 70 successive appearances over eight years.

Wright captained his country on 90 occasions, a joint-record recently broken by Kane, taking in three World Cups with impressive longevity for his era.

He was a true one-club man, winning three league titles, the FA Cup and becoming unofficial "world champions" with Wolves in 1954 - helping inspire the birth of the European Cup - while finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up to Alfredo di Stefano in 1957.

Billy Wright captained England 90 times - a record shared with Bobby Moore until Harry Kane recently surpassed the pair

It feels a little premature to include a 23-year-old with the bulk of his England career ahead of him, but that shows the impact Jude Bellingham has already made for England and Real Madrid.

A Champions League winner, the midfielder has also appeared at four major tournaments for the Three Lions, becoming the youngest player to do so at the delayed Euro 2020, aged 17.

But his role in helping carry England to the final two years ago and a third-place finish at last summer's World Cup really make him stand out.

Bellingham has delivered those moments a nation collectively remembers. The last-gasp overhead kick against Slovakia in 2024, a quickfire double at the Azteca against Mexico this summer and 93rd-minute quarter-final winner against Norway.

His seven goals at this World Cup were more than any previous Three Lions player in a single edition, the solo effort against France a thing of beauty.

The former Birmingham and Dortmund man doesn't turn 24 until June but has already collected 61 England caps and netted 14 times. As Roy Keane put it, Bellingham has the potential to be one of the "greatest of all time".

Ten of Bellingham's 14 England goals have come at major tournaments

In terms of natural ability, Wayne Rooney is among England's greatest ever talents.

Bursting on to the scene at Euro 2004 as an electric 18-year-old, having become England's youngest player and scorer the previous year, convinced fans and media the teen sensation could carry the Three Lions to glory in Portugal.

He bounced World Cup winner Lilian Thuram around in England's opener against France in a glimpse of his precocious strength, before scoring twice against both Switzerland and Croatia.

Who knows how far England would have gone had Rooney not been injured against Portugal in the quarter-final?

He was unable to replicate the impact of his first Euros - a red card at World Cup 2006, suspension for the Euro 2012 group stage, seven goals across six major tournaments - but was an all-rounder who brought more than just goals.

Rooney also won it all with Manchester United, becoming the club's all-time top scorer, and finished his 15-year England career with 53 goals from 120 caps.

Rooney burst on to the scene as an 18-year-old at Euro 2004

There has to be a place for a goalkeeper, and Gordon Banks is the safest pair of hands.

A World Cup winner in 1966, his save from Pele four years later against Brazil is one of the most iconic of all time. Pele called him a "goalkeeper with magic".

Banks spent the majority of his career at Leicester and Stoke, winning a League Cup with each, and earned 73 England caps overall between 1963 and 1972.

His incredible athleticism and reflexes saw the shot-stopper named Fifa's best goalkeeper for five successive years between 1966 and 1971.

Banks and Pele became good friends following the goalkeeper's iconic save in 1970

Gary Lineker's early club career did not deliver the silverware as his goals deserved, netting 40 times but finishing league and FA Cup runner-up in his one season at Everton before joining Barcelona.

He scored a Clasico hat-trick and won the Copa del Rey and Cup Winner's Cup, however, before adding an FA Cup with Tottenham in 1991.

Lineker netted 283 club goals (and famously no cards) in total across spells with Leicester, Everton, Barcelona, Spurs and Nagoya Grampus Eight.

But as a player Lineker is most renowned for his contribution in an England shirt, winning the Golden Boot as they reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1986 - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up that year - before netting another four as the Three Lions reached the semi-finals in 1990.

Lineker equalised against West Germany before England crashed out on penalties.

However, having missed a spot-kick against Brazil, he finished one short of Bobby Charlton's elusive goal record when his international career ended after Euro 92.

Gary Lineker scored 48 goals in 80 games for England

Harry Kane is undoubtedly England's most important and influential player of a generation - it is hard to imagine how this Three Lions side functions once the skipper hangs up his boots.

The Bayern Munich striker, complete with Ballon d'Or, has been scoring goals for his country for almost 12 years, the first just 79 seconds into his debut after coming off the bench against Lithuania in March 2015.

Rooney's goalscoring benchmark is long in his rear view mirror - you wouldn't bank against Kane doubling his nearest rival's figure once his England days are over.

They have come on the biggest stage, too - 21 in 36 appearances from three World Cups and European Championships apiece, winning the World Cup Golden Boot in 2018.

Kane has come closer to winning a major tournament than any England men's captain since Bobby Moore - losing two World Cup semi-finals and back-to-back Euros finals. Team-mate Bellingham called him the "greatest player that has ever played for England".

"I think we'll appreciate him even more in another 10, 15, 20 years when you look back and see what he has achieved," said ex-England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

In many ways, Bobby Moore would be the complete modern-day defender. Cool as you like under pressure, elegant in possession, a great passing range off both feet and, as his West Ham and England team-mate Geoff Hurst said: "Nobody out-ran him and nobody out-jumped him."

Moore's positioning and timing was perfect, that iconic tackle on Jairzinho at the 1970 World Cup the finest example of his poise and precision when defending.

He was also a composed and influential leader. A player built for the big occasions. England boss Sir Alf Ramsey called him: "My lieutenant on the field, a cool, calculated footballer I could trust with my life."

The Barking-born centre-back won the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup with West Ham but his finest moment was leading England to glory in 1966. He was only 25 at the time, having become his country's youngest captain three years earlier.

In 1970, after the Bogota bracelet incident, Moore was imperious as England reached the quarter-finals before bowing out to West Germany.

It was, however, the final group game against Brazil, the most exciting side on the planet, that produced some of the most recognisable and renowned images in sporting history - not only Moore's tackle and Banks' save but the defender swapping shirts with Pele after the final whistle.

"The greatest defender I ever played against," was the Brazilian's verdict.

Bobby Moore is the only man to captain the Three Lions to World Cup glory

For more than a generation, Sir Bobby's England goalscoring record remained unmatched. It took 45 years from his 49th and final strike against Colombia in 1970 until Rooney surpassed him with his half century in 2015.

Charlton was, as Alan Shearer put it, "not only a great goalscorer but a scorer of great goals" and played a pivotal part of the Three Lions' World Cup success in 1966, netting three times on the way to the final.

A scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark long-range strike into the corner at Wembley gave England's campaign lift-off against Mexico, before he scored twice against Eusebio's Portugal in the semi-finals.

Manager Ramsey called the buccaneering midfielder his "lynchpin" as England triumphed over West Germany in the showpiece and those performances helped Charlton win the Ballon d'Or later that year.

He'd be runner-up in successive years after that, too.

Charlton won 106 England caps and was a star for Manchester United, with Rooney also the one to pip his club-record 249 goals for the Old Trafford outfit.

A survivor of the Munich air disaster on 6 February 1958, which killed 23 people including eight players and three members of the club's staff, Charlton won three league titles, an FA Cup and most poignantly the European Cup in 1968.

"England's greatest ever player," Lineker previously told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He was unique. Wherever you go in the world, even if they didn't speak the language, they knew two words - Bobby Charlton."

Arsenal secure crucial draw against wasteful Barcelona in Champions League

It is no mean feat for any team to come away from Camp Nou with a result against Barcelona in the Women's Champions League, let alone a side struggling for form.

With that context in mind, Arsenal's draw on Thursday night was a significant achievement and increases their chances of qualifying for the knockout stages of the competition.

Sitting sixth in the Women's Super League table, their title hopes in tatters, Renee Slegers' side are putting all their eggs in one basket and hoping for success in Europe.

They have a promising eight points from their opening four matches and while giants Lyon await in London next week, their draw with Barca could provide a welcome boost.

Arsenal secure gutsy Champions League draw at Barcelona

Arsenal defender Steph Catley made five interceptions and nine clearances at Camp Nou to deny Barcelona

It was not a scintillating display from Arsenal, nor a tactical masterclass, but it was a gritty showing that we have not seen enough of this season.

With manager Slegers under scrutiny and the players under pressure to perform, the last thing they needed was to face the full-throttle Barcelona attack.

Caroline Graham Hansen's cleverness, Sydney Schertenleib's constant threat and the aura of top scorer Ewa Pajor is enough to strike fear into any team in Europe.

Even with three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati on the bench, Barcelona were able to impose their superiority against a wounded Arsenal – but the Gunners stood firm.

Frida Maanum opened the scoring against the run of play for Arsenal in the first half and they somehow made it to half-time with their lead intact despite 18 shots from their dominant hosts.

Barcelona did continue as expected after the break, equalising through Graham Hansen, but failed to kick on, with Arsenal's experience and maturity showing to see out a draw that ended the Catalan giants' 100% record in this season's Champions League.

"I'm very pleased in general with the players and how they have gone about it, their preparation, ownership and engagement. You know in these games it's about the margins," said Slegers.

"The execution was so good. It is always going to be difficult against Barcelona because they are so good on the ball. It's hard to defend against but we did well.

"We knew there would be opportunities. I'm really pleased with the way we played as it's very different to how we usually play. That we can do it this way [is] a big boost for us as a team.

"We will take that going forward because the next games are coming quickly. It is really difficult to go to Camp Nou. The one point is okay for us, though obviously we went for three."

Criticism of Arsenal this season has centred around their lack of ruthlessness and an inability to turn dominance into winning results.

The tables turned on Thursday as it was Barcelona who were wasteful and frustrating, while Arsenal rode their luck and capitalised where they could.

Defending champions Barcelona had almost 70% possession, 24 shots, 51 touches inside the opposition half and 11 corners but only managed the solitary goal.

Slegers admitted on Tuesday "too many draws" had impacted their start to the season – but was this particular draw proof that the real Arsenal is still hidden among the low confidence and poor form?

"This is a very different game to play but there are of course elements in the performance that we want - and need - to take forward," added Slegers.

"It's there in the team and we need to show that in every single game. If you ask me what words I would use to describe the performance, I would say grit, resilience, clarity, discipline, communication, leadership and bravery as well.

"That is a lot of words but there were a lot of really good things in this performance that we definitely want to build on."

It is a decisive few days for Arsenal with high-flying London City Lionesses up next on Sunday for a game that could impact their hopes of qualifying for next season's Champions League in the battle for a top three spot in the WSL.

Then, they host French giants Lyon in Europe next Thursday before ending the league phase at Inter Milan in December.

UNICEF Rwanda Representative Lieke van de Wiel

Kigali – As grants decline and domestic financing takes over the biggest share of its budget needs, the United Nations is urging the government to protect and sustain funding for children’s sectors.

The call is contained in the FY2026/27 Budget Brief launched on Thursday by UNICEF Rwanda in collaboration with the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning (MINECOFIN). The report examines public spending on education, health, social protection, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH).

The brief says Rwanda’s economy remains resilient, with the national budget rising to Frw 7,796.3 billion for 2026/27, a 12.1 per cent increase from the revised 2025/26 budget. Domestic resources now finance 67.6 per cent of public spending, while external grants account for 7 per cent.

But spending on services that directly benefit children is growing much more slowly.

The combined allocation to education, health, social protection and WASH has increased by only 4.2 per cent to Frw 1,711.3 billion, equivalent to 22 per cent of the national budget. This is below projected inflation of 10.5 per cent, meaning the sectors could have less purchasing power despite receiving more money.

Their share of the national budget has also fallen from 26.8 per cent to 22 per cent over five years. In real terms, the allocation is now lower than it was in 2023/24.

The report warns that this comes at a time when households are facing higher food, energy and housing costs. Food alone accounts for nearly two-thirds of spending among poorer households.

UNICEF Rwanda Representative Lieke van de Wiel said sustained investment in children had already produced measurable results.

“Rwanda has shown what sustained investment in children can achieve. Fewer children are dying before the age of five, more children are completing primary school, and more families have moved out of poverty,” she said.

She said protecting these investments as the government prepares its 2027/28 budget would help build a healthy and skilled workforce needed to achieve Rwanda’s Vision 2050.

Education receives the largest allocation

Jeanette Rwigamba, the Head of National Budget Department at the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning. Economic Planning

Education receives Frw 907.3 billion, making it the largest-funded of the four sectors. About 88 per cent of its budget comes from domestic resources.

However, the brief points to gaps in early childhood education. Pre-primary education, despite recording the fastest growth in enrolment, receives the smallest allocation. One in five primary school pupils also repeats a grade.

UNICEF recommends that countries allocate at least 5 per cent of GDP or 20 per cent of their national budgets to education.

The health sector has been allocated Frw 500.2 billion, a 0.3 per cent decline from the previous year in nominal terms.

Donors still finance 48.4 per cent of the health budget, leaving the sector exposed to changes in external support. Funding for maternal, child and adolescent health has fallen by more than half since 2024/25.

Social protection receives Frw 157.3 billion, making it the only one of the four sectors with an allocation below its 2022/23 level.

Donor funding has fallen by about one-third, forcing the government to increase domestic financing to fill part of the gap. The report warns that this may not be sustainable without deliberate efforts to protect programmes serving vulnerable children and households.

Water, sanitation and hygiene records the strongest budget growth, with its allocation rising by 15.8 per cent to Frw 146.5 billion.

However, about 61 per cent of the sector’s funding still comes from donors, making it the most dependent on external support among the four sectors.

Even with the increase, inflation-adjusted spending per person remains about one-third of what is estimated to be needed to meet the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030.

The report also examines climate-related spending, which amounts to Frw 761.8 billion. But only a small share reaches child-focused sectors. Climate-related allocations account for about 2 per cent of the education budget, less than 1 per cent of social protection and none of the health budget. WASH is the exception, with nearly half of its allocation linked to climate spending.

Government promises to protect investment

MINECOFIN says it wants to strengthen child-focused budgeting and ensure public resources are used to meet children’s needs and protect their rights.

Jeanette Rwigamba, the Head of National Budget Department at the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning. Economic Planning

Jeanette Rwigamba, the ministry’s Head of National Budget Department, said the report would help guide decisions as the government prepares the 2027/28 national budget.

“Investment in people remains one of the key pillars of Rwanda’s development agenda. This report, which we prepared together with UNICEF, provides us with evidence-based information as we prepare the 2027/28 budget. We are committed to working with different ministries and partners to ensure that every franc is used in a way that benefits children,” she said.

The report also points to progress in reducing poverty and improving child health. Poverty fell from 39.8 per cent in 2017 to 27.4 per cent in 2024, while extreme poverty declined from 11.3 per cent to 5.4 per cent.

Stunting among children under five fell from 33 per cent in 2020 to 27 per cent in 2025. Under-five mortality declined from 45 to 36 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2019/20 and 2025.

Pre-primary enrolment also more than doubled, rising from 24.2 per cent in 2021/22 to 50.3 per cent in 2024/25.

Despite these gains, about three in ten children still live in poverty, while 11 districts report stunting rates above 30 per cent.

As preparations for the 2027/28 budget continue, the brief calls for stronger domestic financing for social protection and WASH, continued support for maternal and child health, early childhood education and nutrition programmes, and greater attention to children’s needs in climate-related investments.

It also calls for a balance between spending on economic infrastructure and investment in children, arguing that education, health and social protection are essential to building the skilled and healthy workforce needed for Rwanda’s long-term development.

Government of Rwanda is seeking greater international investment in electricity infrastructure, urban resilience, green industrialisation and climate-smart agriculture as it works to turn its climate commitments into projects that can attract financing and deliver measurable results.

Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva outlined the country’s priorities during several high-level engagements at the COP31 climate conference, where Rwanda called for stronger partnerships with multilateral development banks, development finance institutions and other international partners.

On November 11, Nsengiyumva participated in the High-Level Dialogue on Seizing the Green Industrial Opportunity – Investment, Jobs and Growth for Every Economy.

The discussions examined how countries can use the transition to cleaner economies to attract investment, create jobs and expand industrial capacity. Rwanda highlighted opportunities in renewable energy, clean cooking, electric mobility, sustainable agriculture and the circular economy.

On November 12, the Prime Minister attended the High-Level Event on the Global Grids Accelerator, titled Powering the Future – Grids for Energy Security and Prosperity .

The event was presided over by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres and focused on the role of electricity transmission networks in improving energy security, expanding access and supporting economic growth.

The discussions included the Mission 300 initiative, which aims to connect 300 million people in Africa to electricity by 2030. Rwanda highlighted the need to expand transmission capacity by 70 per cent and increase regional electricity trade from 100 megawatts to 200 megawatts as part of its wider ambitions for the power sector.

The country presented an estimated US$3.05 billion in overall investment needs for its electricity ambitions, including US$1.3 billion for grid infrastructure. It called for greater access to project financing from multilateral development banks and development finance institutions to help deliver the required infrastructure.

Nsengiyumva also participated in a high-level roundtable marking the second decade of the Paris Agreement, which focused on accelerating implementation and improving access to climate finance.

Rwanda outlined its national frameworks, including Vision 2050, the Green Growth and Climate Resilience Strategy and the Rwanda Green Fund, as mechanisms for guiding climate investments. The country also highlighted climate budget tagging and its Green Taxonomy as tools to align public and private financing with environmental priorities.

Rwanda called for climate finance that is more accessible, predictable and responsive to the needs of developing countries, arguing that the implementation of climate commitments depends on the availability of adequate resources.

Urban resilience was another major focus of the Prime Minister’s engagements. At the High-Level Dialogue on Urban Resilience, Adaptation and Climate Action, discussions centred on the growing costs of climate-related risks in cities and the financing required to protect urban populations and infrastructure.

Developing countries are estimated to need more than US$300 billion annually for climate adaptation by 2035. Rwanda presented investments of about US$195 million in Kigali, including the restoration and protection of five wetlands covering approximately 500 hectares. These interventions are intended to reduce flooding risks for more than 220,000 residents.

The country also highlighted the need to strengthen resilience in secondary and satellite cities as urbanisation expands beyond Kigali. Its updated climate commitments under the third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) provide a framework for addressing these challenges.

Rwanda also pointed to international cooperation, including Türkiye’s Sustainable Urban Resilience for the Future Fund (SURFF), as an example of how partnerships can support urban adaptation and resilience programmes.

Agriculture featured in another high-level side event on climate-smart agriculture hosted by the Rwanda Green Fund. The discussions examined how climate investment can protect food production, improve farmers’ livelihoods and strengthen the resilience of agricultural systems.

Rwanda highlighted the Green Gicumbi project, which has supported climate resilience in Gicumbi District and benefited approximately 249,000 people. The initiative combines landscape restoration, sustainable land management and measures to help communities adapt to changing weather conditions.

The country also linked climate-smart agriculture to its wider economic targets under the second National Strategy for Transformation (NST2) and the fifth Strategic Plan for Agriculture Transformation (PSTA5). These include increasing crop productivity by 50 per cent, maintaining agricultural growth above 6 per cent, and doubling agricultural exports and private investment by 2029.

Agriculture accounts for approximately one-fifth of Rwanda’s gross domestic product, making climate resilience in the sector important not only for food security but also for employment, exports and economic growth.

Across the different engagements, Rwanda’s message was that climate commitments must be backed by financing and partnerships capable of delivering projects on the ground. The country is seeking to move beyond policy commitments towards investments in power infrastructure, resilient cities, green industries and agriculture that can support its long-term development ambitions.

MN202611_1sg0zjttw0n.t:
Microsoft is struggling to fix a major global outage of its service that is reportedly affecting tens of thousands of users.

Services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot have been affected by "connectivity problems".

The company said in a series of updates on X that it was seeing "positive results" with its efforts to restore services and that it was rushing to fix the problem.

Reports of issues with Outlook peaked globally at nearly 140,000 around 18:00 GMT on Thursday, according to monitoring website Downdetector. The BBC understands there is no indication the outage was caused by a cyber-attack.

The disruption affects programs that are part of Microsoft 365 - a popular online service among businesses that allows them to use workplace tools like Outlook, Teams and OneDrive.

For international organisations, this platform is essential for connecting and collaborating with colleagues around the world.

Among the issues, users may be unable to view certain files or details on their calendar apps, Microsoft said.

Its AI platform, Copilot, may also be unable to work properly.

Messaging and online meetings were largely functional, the firm added.

Microsoft said on X that the outage was caused by a number of servers "being unexpectedly unavailable", straining its remaining systems.

"We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible," said a Microsoft spokesperson.

The company later warned that some services that had been restored "can become unresponsive again", adding that customers "in any region" could be affected.

Users around the world including the US, Japan and Singapore have reported facing disruptions.

The outage has hit other companies, including AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, which work with Microsoft's systems.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.

Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected the tech giant's suite of productivity tools and companies worldwide.

Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled it to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

MN202611_1sx0dvxtacr.t:
The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack

Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.

Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.

The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.

Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.

Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.

The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.

Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.

Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.

Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."

The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.

"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.

Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.

Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.

Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.

He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.

Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.

Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

Itorero Inganzo Ngari rikomeje imyiteguro y'igitaramo rizizihirizamo imyaka 20 rimaze mu bikorwa byo guteza imbere no gusigasira umuco Nyarwanda binyuze mu nganzo, mu gitaramo gikomeye ryise “Umurage w’Intore”.

Iki gitaramo kizaba ku wa 21 Ugushyingo 2026, kibere muri BK Arena, guhera saa kumi n'ebyiri z'umugoroba (6:00 PM).

Iki gitaramo kigamije kwizihiza urugendo rw’imyaka 20 Inganzo Ngari imaze mu buhanzi, abifuza kuzakitabira bari kugura amatike banyuze ku rubuga rwa www.ticqet.rw cyangwa bagakanda *513*1*02#.

Iri Torero ryashinzwe mu 2006 n'urubyiruko rwari abanyeshuri ariko bari bafite intego yo guteza imbere, kubungabunga no gusigasira umuco Nyarwanda binyuze mu kubyina, kuririmba no gucuranga aho ryatangiranye abaririmbyi n'ababyinnyi bagera kuri 25 mugihe uyu munsi bafite abagera 125.

Kwitwa ‘Inganzo Ngari’, byaturutse ku gitekerezo cyo guhuza abantu batandukanye bafite impano n’urukundo rw’umuco nyarwanda. Nyuma yo kwiyemeza gushyira icyo gitekerezo mu bikorwa, byafunguriye amarembo ababyinnyi baturukaga mu bice bitandukanye by’igihugu ariko abenshi baturutse mu mashuri makuru na za Kaminuza.

Kuva mu 2009, ryakoze ibitaramo bitandukanye byagize uruhare mu guteza imbere umuco Nyarwanda, birimo ikitwa 'Inganzo Twaje' bakoze mu 2009, n’icyo bakoze mu 2010 bise 'Umuco, Kagozi ka Bugingo Kabuza u Rwanda Gucika'.

Mu 2011, bakoze 'Bwiza bwa Mashira Budashira, Irora n’Irongorwa', naho 2013 bakora ikindi bise 'Inzira ya Bene u Rwanda', 2015, bakoze igitaramo bise 'Ruganzu I Bwimba', mu 2018 bakora icyo bise 'Urwamazimpaka', mu gihe mu 2023, basubiye ku rubyiniro mu gitaramo bise 'Ruganzu II Ndoli Abundura u Rwanda'.

Iri torero rifite umwihariko wo kwambara imyenda gakondo yerekana ishusho y’umuco nyarwanda uko wagiye utera imbere. Uretse kubyina, Inganzo Ngari itanga n’umusanzu mu gukomeza kuririmba indirimbo z’umwimerere zishingiye ku muco.

Inganzo Ngari kandi bakomeje kuba itorero rifite igikundiro mu bakunda umuco gakondo, kandi ryagiye ritanga umusanzu ukomeye mu kurinda umuco w’u Rwanda no kuwugeza ku rwego mpuzamahanga.

MN202611_f39xar2trl.t:
Roger Taylor, pictured with bandmates Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Simon le Bon, joined the pop group in 1978

Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor said he will leave the band due to his worsening tinnitus.

Taylor has been the chart-topping group's drummer since they formed in Birmingham in 1978, which he described as "the joy of my life", but said he had "reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors".

The 66-year-old said his condition has been getting steadily worse, leading to him making one of his hardest decisions to quit the band.

The group, made up of Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Nick Rhodes and guitarist John Taylor, said his decision came after "careful consideration and medical advice", which said that "protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first".

Taylor, who left the band in 1985 before returning in 2001, said: "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I'll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they've shown us over the years.

"But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse," he said.

Roger Taylor (left) quit the band in 1985 before returning in 2001

He said deciding on the timing had been difficult but he was pleased to be "going out on a real high".

"We've just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour, which followed our second headline show at BST Hyde Park, our induction into the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame, and a return to the studio with Nile Rodgers.

"I couldn't have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I'll treasure forever.

"I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John," he said.

Taylor's band members added that he had helped define the sound of the group, performing on 10 hit albums, their two number one singles - Is There Something I Should Know? and The Reflex - and the band's 1985 James Bond theme A View To A Kill.

"His drumming helped define the sound of Duran Duran from the very beginning and having him back with us since 2001 has been incredibly important to us all.

"We completely support his decision and wish him health and happiness.

"He will always be part of this family, while we continue exploring new and exciting projects with the band."
