The woman disappeared while on the Marella Voyager (file photo)

The search for a British woman who is believed to have gone overboard from a cruise ship while it was crossing the Atlantic has been suspended, the US Coast Guard (USCG) has said.

The 72-year-old was last seen aboard Tui's Marella Voyager on Monday while the vessel was en route to the Caribbean. Staff realised she was missing on Tuesday, when they noticed her "bed untouched".

USCG said the ship was approximately 500 nautical miles from the area where she was believed to entered the water when it received a missing report.

It added that a coordinated international search and rescue effort had been called off on Wednesday due to factors including "the low likelihood of survival".

USCG said the woman was last recorded accessing a cabin door at about midday on Monday. She is believed to have gone overboard in a remote area of the North Atlantic, roughly 1,400 nautical miles from Bermuda.

In a previous statement, Tui said that after staff realised she was missing, the alarm was raised and a search carried out.

The Daily Mail earlier reported that holidaymakers on board the ship had been told to abandon dinners, drinks and entertainment as the crew carried out an emergency headcount on Tuesday evening.

Passengers stood in lines of four while staff scanned boarding cards to verify the identity of every person on the ship, according to the newspaper.

In a statement, USCG confirmed it had received a missing report at about 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) on Tuesday.

The coast guard said staff also reported that the Marella did not have enough fuel to return to the search area. It is understood that USCG asked the ship to continue its crossing rather than reverse course and search for the woman.

It said that volunteers from the coast guard then worked with search and rescue partners including the Maritime Rescue Coordination Center Delgada and the UK's Joint Rescue Coordination Centre, and issued urgent maritime broadcasts requesting assistance from ships in the area.

It added that multiple commercial vessels were contacted as part of the operation to "consider search opportunities, but none were in the vicinity".

Search efforts were suspended at about 15:50 EST (20:50 GMT) on Wednesday, "after considering the extensive search area, the elapsed time between the presumed incident and notification, the lack of available search assets in the remote location, negative results from maritime broadcasts, the sea state, and the low likelihood of survival", the coast guard said.

The Marella Voyager, carrying around 2,000 passengers and 800 crew, left Malaga on 4 November and is due to arrive in Antigua on Friday before calling at Dominica and finishing its voyage in Barbados on Sunday.

A spokeswoman for Marella Cruises earlier said it was supporting the authorities with their enquiries. It added it was "deeply saddened" by the disappearance, adding: "Our thoughts are with the guest's loved ones at this very difficult time.

A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said in an earlier statement: "We are supporting the family of a British national reported missing on a cruise ship in the Atlantic Ocean and we are in touch with the relevant authorities."

In a separate case, a cruise ship pianist was found treading water on Sunday around 20 miles off the Californian coast after falling overboard.

Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

MN202611_xgc3cw4ztq.t:
Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow was the latest of many trips the US envoys have made to see Vladimir Putin

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held a fresh round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest discussions aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

The pair are now in Dublin to meet Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Witkoff said a new round of trilateral talks had already been agreed with Putin.

But in a sign of further tension, Zelensky said on Thursday morning that Ukraine's military was again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

The peace talks in the Emirates were framed as being centred around European security arrangements in a post-war scenario, although a resolution to the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 still appears distant.

Comments by both President Vladimir Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.

Witkoff said that Europeans would join the next round of talks. "They are our partners and it's important to us that they take part," Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham had said that UK national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join Zelensky, Witkoff and Kushner for talks in Dublin, but Downing Street later said they had been delayed, meaning the national security adviser could no longer join.

Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side but added "some things" were already clear: "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going." He did not elaborate further.

Starshield was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use. Along with Starlink, it has come to play a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line. A similar issue with connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed and it remained unclear who had ordered the temporary restrictions.

Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".

Meanwhile, some of the longstanding roadblocks in the peace process were addressed during the US-Russia talks in the Kremlin.

The territorial issue continues to be a key point of contention, Putin said.

"For us there is only one line of demarcation: the line of the state border. Because then it will be clear that we are here, and you are there. As soon as we start discussing 'grey zones'… arguments immediately start and any agreements become unstable. And there will be no lasting peace."

He also suggested organising a humanitarian truce to allow for the evacuation of hundreds of civilians from a frontline area, on the model of last month's ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

Putin suggested a similar five-day ceasefire for Kostyantynivka, a contested front-line Ukrainian city in the eastern region of Donetsk.

Kyiv disputes that Russia fully holds the town, and a truce could help Moscow's troops to make a final push to seize it.

"Considering that they brought in equipment and rotated troops in Oleshky under the guise of a humanitarian operation, it's clear what they want in Kostyantynivka," Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmitry Lytvyn told the BBC, adding that the details would need to be "clarified".

But at the core of this week's talks has been the issue of European security architecture. Earlier Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said it was "clear that the current system does not work."

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin and that decisions about their continent could be made without them.

Zelensky said he found the US approach of discussing a new European security order with Russia "a bit strange".

"It is a significant shift in the US position that the US has now taken on board the Russian demand that the European security architecture needs to be discussed and agreed upon in parallel with the Ukraine peace talks," said the Director of the Estonian Foreign Policy Institute Kristi Raik.

She said the Russians have a "long history" of wanting to revise European security architecture, intended as core principles "like sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principle that there is no use of force to some conflicts".

Russia "has long looked to reduced Nato presence on the Eastern flank and that… get some kind of veto rights in decisions concerning European security and defence," Raik said. "And that's where it gets even more difficult to imagine that there could be an agreement between the Europeans and the Russians."

On Thursday, Putin again repeated that the presence of foreign troops in Ukraine was "unacceptable" to Russia, and said Russia would like the Americans to engage with Europe "so that the Europeans can decide what they truly want: peace or war".

During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.

That position has now shifted for many as concern that decisions about the European continent could be made without European involvement.

Kushner also urged Europe to "identify one person to speak on their behalf" in the negotiations.

Top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas told the BBC's Newshour programme the presence of a European official at the next meeting showed the Kremlin had "now realised that Europe is a big player here because we are the ones who have been supporting Ukraine".

With financial pressures on European budgets, Kallas said it was "becoming harder to help Ukraine", but warned of the "the danger not only for the eastern flank of the European Union but actually for our whole continent" if Russian aggression was allowed to continue.

The Kremlin has not confirmed the make-up of next week's talks, and at the start of the meeting, Putin had indicated he didn't want European countries to play a full role. The Russians have long cited Europe's support for Kyiv as an obstacle to their involvement.

Speaking to Kushner and Witkoff, Putin said he was encouraging them "to work with your European allies so that they finally decide whether they want peace or war in Ukraine."

The president of Kenya William Ruto on Thursday morning hosted heads of European Union Delegations to African countries at State House Nairobi.

The convergence comes at a time the East African state marks 50 years of diplomatic relations with the European Union.

“We have agreed to elevate our relations into a comprehensive strategic partnership anchored in multilateralism, international law, democratic governance and sustainable development,” Ruto told the Diplomats.

President Ruto outlined Kenya’s economic relations with the EU, noting, “the EU accounts for 21% of Kenya’s global exports, making it our largest export market.”

He said his government is committed to translating the Economic Partnership Agreement into greater trade and investment opportunities, while addressing barriers facing our exporters, particularly smallholder producers.

“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to peace and security, appreciating the EU’s support for African Union-led missions, including in Somalia, and its €20 million (KSh3 billion) contribution towards strengthening the Kenya Defence Forces,” Ruto said.

MTN Rwanda has launched MTN One TV, a digital entertainment platform that brings different forms of entertainment together in one application while creating opportunities for local content creators to showcase their talents and reach wider audiences.

The platform, officially unveiled on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, offers users access to a variety of entertainment content, including romantic stories, comedy and cooking programmes, providing a single destination for audiences to discover and enjoy content.

Beyond offering entertainment to subscribers, MTN One TV is expected to support Rwanda’s growing creative industry by providing local content creators with another platform to showcase their productions, connect with audiences and expand their reach.

Speaking at the launch, MTN Rwanda’s Chief Executive Officer, Monzer Ali, reflected on his early connection with the television industry, recalling how he earned his first income as a child by helping neighbours repair television antennas.

“My first income was when I was seven years old from the entertainment industry, from the same television that Manjot talked about,” he said, explaining how he and two other children would climb rooftops to adjust antennas so families could watch television.

Ali said the experience, although far removed from his current role, made the launch of MTN One TV particularly meaningful.

“From there, today I am here after a few years launching MTN One TV,” he said, drawing a connection between his childhood experience and the company’s entry into digital entertainment.

The launch marks MTN Rwanda’s expansion beyond its traditional telecommunications and mobile money services into digital entertainment, as the company seeks to become part of a wider ecosystem connecting technology, audiences and content producers.

The event brought together the Minister of State in charge of ICT and Innovation, the Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Youth and Arts, media representatives and local content creators.

The platform is expected to contribute to the development of Rwanda’s creative economy by giving emerging and established creators additional opportunities to distribute their work and reach viewers through digital channels.

For MTN Rwanda, the launch also signals an ambition to make entertainment more accessible while creating new opportunities for local talent in an increasingly digital media landscape.

Thomas Tuchel has been England head coach since January 2025

England head coach Thomas Tuchel says he has "no intention" of leaving the job before Euro 2028 regardless of any offers from major clubs.

Tuchel succeeded Gareth Southgate as England boss in 2025 and signed an extension in February until Euro 2028, which will be co-hosted by England.

Manchester United are in advanced talks with USA men's coach Mauricio Pochettino over replacing Michael Carrick as head coach.

The Red Devils will need to activate a release clause in Pochettino's contract to hire the Argentine, believed to be in the region of around £7m.

But Tuchel says his contract does not include a release clause and he does not intend to leave his role to return to club management.

"I signed the contract, I want to stay until the Euros," he said. "I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business."

England lost the past two Euros finals under Southgate before Tuchel led the Three Lions to the semi-finals of his first major tournament, this summer's World Cup.

However, the former Bayern Munich, Chelsea and Paris St-Germain boss did say that he would return to club football after seeing out his England contract.

"I miss the 50 matches [a season]," he said.

"I miss the two minutes when everything is done. You go out two minutes before the whistle goes, it's like the best two minutes, everything is done and you're in a full stadium, lights are on and you're just so excited and you're part of it."

England are second in their Nations League group and have two more group games over the coming days.

Tuchel's side host Croatia on Thursday before facing World Cup winners and group leaders Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

Northern Ireland play Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday before travelling to Budapest to face Hungary on Tuesday

Across his two spells as Northern Ireland boss, Michael O'Neill has been blessed with no shortage of centre-back talent.

Jonny Evans, Aaron Hughes, Gareth McAuley and Craig Cathcart were mainstays of his first stint in charge - so much so that, in some of the biggest games of O'Neill's managerial career at Euro 2016, the quartet all started across a flat back-four.

Since returning to the job four years ago, O'Neill has switched to three at the back, with Sunderland duo Trai Hume and Dan Ballard providing an injection of Premier League quality in what remains a side largely drawn from the Championship and League One.

But with Hume, something of a Swiss army knife in the squad, covering the injured Conor Bradley on the right flank and even starting in centre midfield against Ukraine last month, and Ballard presently nursing an injured hamstring, change has been required through this Nations League campaign.

Despite those forced alterations in defence, the side go into their concluding Group B2 fixtures against Ukraine and Hungary top of their pool and the only side at any level of the competition yet to concede a goal.

At the heart of their defensive efforts have been Ruairi McConville and Tom Atcheson, two young centre-backs already described by their international manager as having "no ceiling" .

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

NI can draw on strong club form in key window

At 21-years-old, Norwich City's McConville is the more senior of the pair.

Having been given his debut off the bench at home to Belarus two years ago this week, among the former Brighton man's early international assignments was trying to keep a rampant Alexander Isak in check during a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.

In the short time since he has looked an increasingly commanding figure, leading this Nations League group in clearances made with both head and boot.

"It would be unbelievable to keep that record for these last two games and go the whole of the campaign," he said of what is Northern Ireland's longest run without conceding a goal since 2017.

McConville notes that the streak is a team effort and product of collective work-rate, rather than just the defensive three alone.

"We're a team that works hard, a team that doesn't want to give anything up.

"We're confident in ourselves and we know that we're a good side."

It is McConville who has taken on the Ballard role in the middle of the defence for the past three games, with Atcheson on the right and Oxford United's Ciaron Brown, himself superb through the campaign so far, playing from the left.

On the developing understanding between an emerging unit, McConville added: "We're enjoying playing together.

"It's still early days together and we have to keep taking it game by game and doing what the gaffer tells us and the work on the training pitch.

"We don't have much time together when we're here [in international camp] so it's important to do all we can."

Atcheson's comfort on the ball has been an asset across his six caps

After 16 caps, McConville is a relative veteran compared to Atcheson, who made his international bow in a friendly against Wales in March at a time when he had only four senior club starts to his name at Blackburn Rovers.

The most recent of those had come under O'Neill, then in a short stint as caretaker manager at the Championship club.

Clearly impressed by what he saw from the now 20-year-old at Ewood Park, Atcheson made his first Northern Ireland start against Guinea in June, a game in which he scored the winner with a fabulous flick before later being shown a red card.

Some 428 minutes into his international career, Atcheson is still to experience what it feels like to concede a goal.

The England-born defender feels Ballard "is definitely a big miss" to the side, but believes the squad's understanding of O'Neill's desired system is an asset to those who have starred during the Sunderland man's latest absence.

"I feel like everyone knows what they need to do, everyone knows their job, the details of the formation we play and system," he said.

"That's so key and I think that's why we're so solid defensively.

"It's a team thing, we're set up right, we're very on it all the time and everyone gives their all."

MN202611_19283me1038.t:
The school's head teacher has been arrested to assist with investigations

Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.

The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.

The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.

According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.

Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.

Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.

A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.

The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.

Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.

The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.

The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.

Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.

The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

The USA reached the last 32 of last year's Under-17 World Cup, the first of five successive editions to be held annually in Qatar

The USA have withdrawn from the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar because of the risk of armed conflict.

In a letter sent to players and seen by news agency Reuters, US Soccer said it made the decision "in light of current circumstances".

It cited advice from the US Department of State, which issued a level three travel advisory , external for Qatar last month.

That came a day after Yemen's Houthi movement carried out a deadly attack on an airport in neighbouring Saudi Arabia, while air strikes have continued on Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

The 48-team tournament runs from 19 November to 13 December, and the USA were due to play group games against Montenegro, Chile and Algeria.

The US travel advisory mentioned Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure, and warned that hostilities "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area".

The update told Americans to reconsider travel to Qatar because of "risk of armed conflict".

"The well-being of our players and staff will always be our top priority," US Soccer said in the letter.

It said it would notify the players' clubs and asked players not to comment publicly until their withdrawal has been announced by tournament organisers Fifa.

The 2027 Asian Cup - Asia's version of the European Championships - was due to take place in Saudi Arabia from 7 January to 5 February, but has been postponed by almost a year because of the conflict.

The wife of England striker Ollie Watkins, who plays in the Saudi Pro League, has taken their children back to the UK until the situation "calms down".

Computer programming and consultancy services in particular contributed to overall growth (generic photo)

The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures , external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

Although investors have recently been concerned about slower artificial intelligence development in the US and the long term viability of AI firms' business models, businesses have continued to invest in the technologies.

Sarah Coles, from investment platform AJ Bell, said that since the start of the year, "it's the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth" noting that these are the areas benefitting from the increasing use of AI.

The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise".

A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said.

High energy costs have been stoked by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

US and Israeli attacks led to Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz - a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas.

Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other's oil refineries, leading to a squeeze on global refining capacity, hitting diesel and petrol prices.

What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you?

Entrepreneur Richard Benc says the UK watch market and exports have been surprisingly resilient

Richard Benc, founder of mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, says sales are better than he expected.

"We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says.

The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches.

MN202611_7mrle8nkry.t:
Andy Robertson is one of two centurions for Scotland men

Andy Robertson says it gives him "goosebumps" any time he thinks about it.

Friday at Hampden, North Macedonia the visitors, a 102nd cap to be won and, when it is, he'll be level in the pantheon with Sir Kenny Dalglish, the football man he loves more than any other.

On Monday in St Gallen, Switzerland - all being well - Robertson will break the great man's record, a mark that has stood for 40 years.

The Tottenham left-back is sitting in the boardroom at Queen's Park in the shadow of Hampden with a phone in his hand and eyes fixed on his 19-year-old self coming off the bench in Warsaw on 5 March, 2014.

"Nervous, excited, living the dream, not knowing what road I was on," he smiles as he looks at the moment he takes his first touch in international football.

"As I was going on, Gordon [Strachan, Scotland manager] said to me, 'remember why you're here, play like you play at Dundee United, don't play safe'. The first ball, when it came to me, I just drove forward about 30, 40 yards.

"I had pretty much every emotion that day. My mum and dad were there. My brother. My aunt and uncle. My other uncle. There's a picture of me and my brother [Stephen] at the airport after the game. He had a big Poland hat on and a half-and-half scarf. He was well oiled by that point."

Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia

Robertson says he'd have laughed out loud had you told him then what lay ahead of him - two Premier Leagues, two League Cups, an FA Cup, a Champions League, a Super Cup, a Club World Cup, soon-to-be the most capped male Scottish players in history and, by a mile, the one with the most games as captain of the men's team.

"I've never actually been confident," he says, which is a surprise admission given everything he's done.

Maybe what he means is that he always had a quiet belief in his own ability but found that constantly questioning himself was who he was and who maybe who he still is.

"I've always doubted myself and that's always got the best out of me. I've always tried to prove people wrong and prove myself wrong. The one thing I didn't do was look too far ahead. I always just lived in the here and now and that's served me well."

In the room where he's talking there are a dozen normal chairs and away to the side, detached from the rest, is an elaborate seat. A high-backed, ornate, somewhat regal affair.

It looks fit for a king and, given the history Robertson's about to make, maybe he should plonk himself in it. And that brings us back to the man whose record he's about to match and surpass.

"There are normal seats but there's one throne and Kenny Dalglish should be sat on it," he says. "Friday night's not about me. Friday night's about the greatest player of all time in our country, and for me, that will always be Kenny.

You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career

"He's had this record for so long. He deserves it. If he played in a different era, he would probably have played a number of games that wouldn't have been able to be caught.

"Sometimes - not as a criticism - as a country we're maybe not good at recognising how good people we've got are. For me, he's the best player to ever play with Scotland and arguably Britain.

"We have to appreciate that man because I certainly do, my family certainly do and, I think on Friday, I'll have him at the front of my mind, the back of my mind and I'm not really bothered about myself."

It's a lovely thing, that. Robertson, about to draw level with Dalglish, is only thinking about Dalglish.

The depth of feeling comes tumbling out of him when he starts telling stories about what King Kenny means to his family and how he seemingly created a miracle by momentarily curing Robertson's beloved late grandfather's hearing.

"I always remember my agent talking to me about the first time he met Liverpool," Robertson says of a time when he was still with Hull but about to move to Anfield.

"He met the chief scout and sporting director and all of a sudden Kenny 'accidentally' walked into the room. It was 100% planned, I know it was planned.

You can watch Tom English's interview with Andy Robertson on the BBC Scottish Football YouTube channel HERE , external

"One of the things right at the top of the list for me was the fact [by joining Liverpool] I got to meet Kenny in person and I've actually got to have a relationship with him and his family, because his family are special.

"My dad, in particular, has met people in football through me, but I've never seen him being starstruck by anyone apart from Kenny.

"I always remember, we'd just beaten Barcelona 4-0 [in May, 2019] to qualify for my second Champions League final. My grandad was at the game and I managed to grab Kenny afterwards. I says, 'Kenny, would you mind coming in to see my grandad and my uncle? They would love to see you'.

"Bear in mind his grandson's just qualified for another Champions League final and he basically barged me out of the way and shook Kenny's hand.

"My grandad had hearing aids. He couldn't really hear much of us but he heard everything Kenny said, so it did open a lot of questions in the family as to how bad the ear problem was with my grandad. He's no longer with us but to see how happy he was… Kenny was his hero."

When Robertson moved to Liverpool for the hilariously small sum of £8m in 2017, his wife, Rachel, was expecting their first child. The Dalglishes, he says, helped so much that he could hardly ever repay them for their support and friendship.

On the pitch and off, the transfer to Liverpool as a 23-year-old was the greatest move he could have possibly made.

In reflective mood, on the cusp of Scottish football history, Robertson talks about his mother and father and his brother. "They're as proud of my brother as they are of me," he said. "The exact same, whatever achievements we have. But I think they're more proud of the men we've become. That was always most important for me.

"Anyone who knows me, my family, my friends, I always want them to like the person first, the footballer second. Anyone that only wants to know me as the footballer, then I don't let them get too close but if they want to know me as the person first and foremost, then they're the people that are really in my close circle.

"I've still got the same friends I went to nursery with at three years old. Three of my best friends."

Inside the fairytale journey of Scotland captain Robertson

Robertson hits 100 Scotland caps - but which other men make top 10?

Robertson says he often thinks about the game in Scotland and whether young kids today are getting the kind of opportunities he got. "We talk about that - my story, John McGinn's story, Ryan Christie's story," Robertson said.

"There'll be a hundred people going, 'I could have been that'. Football has a lot to do with ability and mentality, but also you need a little bit of luck as well.

"It's about trying to protect the 15, 16, 17-year-olds just now and we all have a duty to help with that. We always want the young players to come in and I just love their energy, I love how excited they are. Findlay Curtis just bounces about all the time.

"These are the kids that are going to bring the country forward. They're all sitting at the other end of the table playing games we don't even know about but it's great for us to sit back and go, 'OK, we're part of this squad, but when we leave, then hopefully Scotland will be in a good place."

To Friday, then. A record-equaller but, to Robertson, this is no nostalgia trip. This is a game Scotland desperately want - and need - to win.

He says they were a yard off it in all areas last time out against Slovenia. "Unacceptable," he recalled. "We didn't give our fans anything to shout about."

He departs with fighting words about the desire within the squad to make amends. Out the door, down the corridor and onwards into history. Seconds later, he returns. "Forgot my washbag," he laughed. "Bet Kenny didn't have one of these!"

Glasgow, Liverpool, Scotland - the ties that bind.

MN202611_n2uizbmgdx.t:
Jude Bellingham shared an old photo of him and brother Jobe after England's squad announcement last week

It is six years since Jude Bellingham played his final game for Birmingham City, and three years since younger brother Jobe wore the club's shirt for the last time.

While Jude, 23, is establishing himself as a footballing great at European greats Real Madrid following a spell at Borussia Dortmund, Jobe, 21, is continuing his football education at his brother's former club in Germany after two seasons with Sunderland.

The Stourbridge-born midfielders have moved on with their careers.

Their memories, however, live on at St Andrew's, such was the impact the boyhood Birmingham fans made in the Championship.

On match days supporters stop and pose for photographs in front of Jude's mural outside the ground. Fans still turn up to matches wearing Bellingham shirts.

"They both had a real connection with fans," Craig Courtney, from the Tilton Talk fan podcast, told BBC Sport. "Fans loved the fact they both cared.

"They wore their hearts on their sleeves and helped Birmingham when we were fighting relegation. Even now, Jude and Jobe remember where it all started for them."

The brothers played 70 league and cup games between them for Birmingham after graduating from the academy.

They have never appeared together in a senior match, however, as Jude - who joined Birmingham aged eight - had left by the time Jobe broke into the first team in 2022.

The Bellinghams will become the first brothers to play for England for 19 years if Jobe wins his first cap and appears alongside Jude, a veteran of 60 appearances, in the Nations League game with Croatia at Wembley.

"It will be an incredibly proud moment for Birmingham City if that happens," said Courtney.

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

Listen: How Jude Bellingham became a global brand

Birmingham supporters have had little to cheer about recently.

It is 15 years since they last appeared in the Premier League, while the 2011 League Cup winners even dipped down to League One recently.

While fierce rivals Aston Villa were playing - and beating - Bayern Munich and Bologna in the Champions League two years ago, Birmingham were losing at Shrewsbury and drawing with Northampton Town.

Yet the mood is changing at St Andrew's.

After 15 games Birmingham sit top of the Championship and there are plans for a new 62,000-capacity stadium in time for 2030-31.

"As a club, we've been right down in the doldrums," added Courtney. "Now we're top of the table and having a new stadium built.

"There is an argument that none of this would have been possible without the fees received for Jude and Jobe."

A mural tribute to Jude Bellingham outside St Andrew's

Jude is the youngest player in Birmingham's history after making his debut aged 16 years and 38 days in 2019.

Clubs across Europe were pursuing him when he signed his first professional contact in 2020 after turning 17 - a deal both he and Birmingham knew would never be fulfilled.

His actions, however, ensured Birmingham would receive a significant transfer fee when he left, and soon afterwards he joined Dortmund for an initial fee of £20m during the Covid-19 pandemic.

When he joined Real in 2023, Birmingham received a reported sell-on fee of at least £10m. , external

"We cannot possibly imagine, without Jude's decision [to sign a contract], where we would be as a club in a pandemic like this," then Birmingham chief executive Xuandong Ren told BBC WM after Jude joined Dortmund.

"He could easily have just looked after himself and not the club, but he chose the best possible way to look after the club."

Jobe became the second youngest player to play for Birmingham when he made his debut in January 2022 aged 16 years and 107 days.

"This was a lad, regardless of who his brother was or what he was achieving, who would do anything to write his own success story," former Birmingham striker Troy Deeney, who played in the game when Jobe made his debut, told the Sun. , external

"Everything he has achieved on the pitch, too, has come with an instant comparison to his older brother.

"He never got that one moment to enjoy something without someone, somewhere saying: 'Yeah, but what about Jude?'

"That only added to how strong he was mentally, and anyone who suggests he is where he is because of his last name is talking rubbish."

Deeney added: "What impressed me more than anything he had done on the pitch was his attitude - a hell-bent determination to get to the top and the common sense to take all the right steps along the way."

Jobe played 26 games before Sunderland paid £3m for him in 2023, with Birmingham receiving a reported £4m sell-on fee when he moved to Dortmund two years later.

Although significantly less than the fees generated by his brother, it was nevertheless welcome revenue.

Jobe Bellingham was given his Birmingham City debut by manager Lee Bowyer in January 2022

Both Jude and Jobe have returned to St Andrew's since their transfers.

Jobe captained England Under-21s to a 2-0 win against the Republic of Ireland at his old ground last November.

Before that match U21s boss Lee Carsley, who managed Jude when he was England interim manager in 2024, praised the brothers for their work ethic and determination to be the best.

Carsley said: "I know how much they love the Blues still and how important the club is to them."

Jude, tipped to be a future England captain, was at St Andrew's in July watching his former club in a pre-season friendly against Barcelona. He even wore a Birmingham shirt while watching from the stands.

Jude wore a Birmingham City shirt when he returned to St Andrew's

When Jude joined Dortmund in 2020 Birmingham retired the 17-year-old's number 22 shirt after 44 appearances.

"That was a gesture of thanks for what Jude had done," said Courtney.

"It might be wishful thinking, but I really believe Jude has unfinished business at Birmingham. I can see a scenario before he retires where he gets an opportunity to wear the number 22 again."

Should the Bellingham brothers play together against Croatia, they will become the first siblings to appear for England since Gary and Phil Neville against Spain in a friendly at Old Trafford in 2007.

It will be an immensely proud moment for their parents, Mark and Denise.

"We've played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life," Jude, a Champions League and La Liga winner with Real Madrid, wrote on social media , external in 2024.

"That would mean more than any of the trophies. Nothing would even get close to that... nothing."

Esmee Brugts has made more than 100 appearances for Barcelona after joining in 2023

Barcelona's team is markedly different to the one Arsenal faced in the 2025 Women's Champions League final - but the challenge is as difficult as ever.

Three-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas was among a number of high-profile summer departures, but Barca remain favourites to continue their European domination.

The reigning champions have won all three league-phase matches, scoring 19 goals, and welcome Arsenal to the Nou Camp on Thursday (17:45 GMT).

Two seasons ago, Arsenal stunned Barcelona in the Women's Champions League final , less than five months after Renee Slegers was named permanent manager.

That victory kick-started a new era for the Gunners under Slegers, but it has not gone to plan so far this season.

Disappointing results and a five-game winless run, which ended in October, have left Arsenal sixth in the Women's Super League.

However, the Gunners have started the European campaign well and are fifth in the table with seven points from their first three matches.

And given Barcelona's summer changes, Arsenal might have hoped to be facing a team in transition - but the Spanish giants look as strong as ever.

So how have Barca - who have won four of the past six Women's Champions League titles - hit the ground running this term despite losing some of their key players?

When Spain great Putellas left Barcelona in the summer to join London City Lionesses, it felt like the end of an era.

She was followed to Bromley by defender Mapi Leon, while full-back Ona Batlle joined Arsenal and Salma Paralluelo swapped Barcelona for European rivals Lyon.

All four had played a key part in Barcelona's dominance and ended their time at the club with a historic quadruple, including a fourth Champions League last season.

So how have Barcelona coped with losing such big players?

"Every season is different. There are always changes but we know that's football," Barcelona's Esmee Brugts told BBC Sport.

"There's an opportunity to make a new story and that's up to us. So far, I've been quite happy with how it's going.

"I'm excited for the upcoming games to see how we do. It can be a bit different - but different in a good way also."

Barcelona's success is down to multiple factors, but it all centres around a distinctive playing identity that is ingrained in Spanish footballers from a young age.

Stars such as three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati were developed at the club's famous La Masia youth academy, situated next to the Estadi Johan Cruyff, which is named after one of Barca's greatest footballers.

They produce a conveyor belt of talent, all trained to play the same way, and having learned to swap in and out of positions seamlessly.

It is a way of playing that Netherlands international Brugts has picked up with ease since joining in 2023.

"It's difficult to explain because it's so many small things. It's doing the simple things good," said Brugts. "It's a team sport. If everybody does their own roles, you'll perform the best way.

"I watched a documentary about Johan Cruyff and it's exactly how he wanted to play. It's how we try to play every week. We try to be as perfect as possible.

"We try to win every trophy there is by playing really beautiful football, in my opinion. The 'tiki-taka' I enjoy so much."

Barcelona beat rivals Real Madrid 7-0 last month in Liga F

Arsenal boss Slegers said Barcelona have "a really strong identity" and she does not believe this changes when new players come into the side.

"They can play in different positions and also have a very strong and clear way of playing. It's very impressive with the way Barcelona plays," said Slegers.

"With new players coming in and then rotating, their style of play stands up. We think we have quite a clear idea of what that could look like."

While it is a new era for Barcelona, their ambitions remain the same - to defend their four titles this season.

Brugts said they are "really building" their identity with new players in the squad and believe there are "no limits" to what they can produce.

Talented youngsters such as midfielder Clara Serrajordi, 18, defender Renee van Asten, 20, and forward Vicky Lopez, 20, have added more depth to the squad.

"It took me some time to adjust, to learn and understand what it is to play the Barca way. I'm still not there, but it's a process," said 23-year-old Brugts.

"It's an interesting journey - to do it surrounded by the best players, some that have left and some that are still here.

"I'm super-grateful and I'm super-proud if I look at what's coming up from the younger teams. I'm very impressed with how good they are.

"The way Barcelona plays is something you have to learn when you are young. Whenever we need them, they are ready to play and understand the game."

"Amazing" Kane targets 100 international goals

Harry Kane will become England's most capped player against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday.

The 33-year-old Ballon d'Or winner has scored a record 91 goals in 125, soon to be 126, matches for his country.

We look at 10 of his most iconic moments in an England jersey - not counting the moment he almost lost his voice in a BBC interview after the summer's World Cup quarter-final win over Mexico.

England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender

Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record

Harry Kane scored with just his third touch in international football

Kane started his England career with a goal after just 79 seconds and three touches - in a 4-0 Euro 2016 qualifying win over Lithuania in March 2015.

Then 21 and in his first season as a Tottenham regular, he came on in the 70th minute before heading in Raheem Sterling's cross at Wembley.

The BBC match report called him "the man with the Midas touch in front of goal this season".

Harry Kane was England captain at his second major tournament, the 2018 World Cup

Kane has scored 21 major tournament goals for England, which is a record.

His first two - having failed to bag at Euro 2016 - came against Tunisia at the 2018 World Cup as captain.

He netted the opener after John Stones' header was saved and nodded in a stoppage-time winner to give England a 2-1 win in Volgograd, Russia.

Harry Kane has scored four goals against Panama at World Cups

Kane's first England hat-trick came in their next game, a 6-1 win over Panama in the World Cup in Nizhny Novgorod.

He scored two penalties and then deflected in Ruben Loftus-Cheek's shot for probably one of his easiest career hat-tricks.

Harry Kane finished two goals ahead of anyone else at the 2018 World Cup

That summer Kane became the second Englishman to win a World Cup Golden Boot, after Gary Lineker, with six goals.

The sixth was his penalty to give England a 1-0 lead over Colombia in the last 16.

Colombia equalised but Kane also scored in the shootout to help the Three Lions through.

Harry Kane made England's win over Germany safe at the Covid-delayed Euro 2020

Kane was again involved in the goals as England beat Germany in a knockout game for the first time in 55 years, to reach the Euro 2020 quarter-finals in 2021.

The striker nodded in from Jack Grealish's cross with four minutes remaining to seal a 2-0 win at Wembley.

Harry Kane was denied by former Leicester team-mate Kasper Schmeichel but netted the rebound at Euro 2020

One of the biggest goals of Kane's career was the extra-time winner over Denmark to take them into the Euro 2020 final.

His penalty was saved by Denmark's Kasper Schmeichel but the rebound came back to him to score in a 2-1 Wembley win.

That was England's first men's major tournament final since the 1966 World Cup.

Harry Kane overtook Wayne Rooney's England scoring record at the age of 29

Kane became England's all-time record goalscorer with his 54th goal in March 2023, taking him past Wayne Rooney, with their first away win against Italy since 1964.

He scored a first-half penalty as the Three Lions started their Euro 2024 qualifying campaign with a 2-1 win in Naples.

The striker has since extended that record by another 37 goals.

Harry Kane was the joint top scorer at Euro 2024 with three goals

England fell behind early on in their Euro 2024 semi-final match against the Netherlands in Dortmund.

But then Kane equalised from the spot in the first half - before Ollie Watkins' last-minute winner to take them to the final.

It was his second European Championship semi-final goal in two attempts

Harry Kane was awarded a golden cap before his 100th cap

Kane was awarded a golden cap and wore golden boots to mark his 100th England appearance in a Nations League match against Finland in 2024.

And he marked the occasion with both goals in a 2-0 win at Wembley, smashing an effort in off the underside of the bar and then curling in a second.

Kane scores late winner as England overcome DR Congo to reach last 16

England's 2026 World Cup campaign almost ended with a last-32 embarrassment against DR Congo.

But Kane stepped up to save them with two goals in the final 15 minutes.

He headed in the equaliser before smashing in a brilliant winner on the turn with four minutes remaining.

In the next round he netted against Mexico and made headlines with a squeaky-voiced post-match interview in the Azteca altitude...

Residents in King's Lynn are campaigning for more green space to be protected

After a successful campaign getting parkland protected, residents in a Norfolk town are asking for more space to be given the same safeguards from development.

Seven acres (2.8 hectares) of land known as Harding's Pits, beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, will be preserved after it was given "village green status" by the county council .

The Harding's Pits Community Association had campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as leisure space.

Next, the group wants the protection to be extended to the east side, which has been earmarked for up to 50 houses in King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council's local plan , external . The authority has been approached for comment.

The land in the foreground has been given protected status, but the space closer to the town centre at the top has been earmarked for housing

Alexandra Kemp, an independent councillor, said she was asking her authority to amend its local plan.

She said: "I want to protect the east side of Hardings Way as a village green. To take out the 50 houses earmarked for Harding's Pits east from the borough's local plan, and provide community sports facilities, more trees and places for wildlife instead.

"Any development along Hardings Way risks more general traffic which would be devastating to the peace, quiet, safety, and amenity and wildlife."

The local council has been given a target to build more than 10,000 new homes by 2040 by the government.

Harding's Pits is located alongside the River Great Ouse

Harding's Pits was turned into a public space in the early 1960s, but was originally a 19th Century clay pit which was then used as landfill.

The site is currently used for dog walking and as pedestrian access to King's Lynn town centre.

Sculptures of bears and bees will be displayed across Jersey

A new public art trail will mark the arrival of Asiatic black bears, Jersey Zoo has said.

Sculptures of bears and bees would be put up across the island's wild landscapes, coastal spots and urban spaces to celebrate the arrival of the new species in their new enclosure next year, said bosses.

They said the installation, which launches in July next year, aimed to shine a light on "connections that sustain the natural world, from its largest inhabitants to its smallest".

Artists will be invited to submit designs to turn the sculptures into "distinctive works of art" while schools and community groups will also be encouraged to participate.

It is hoped the sculptures will then be sold a fundraising auction at the end of the summer.

Rebecca Brewer, chief executive of Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, said: "We want everyone who connects with our work, whether at Jersey Zoo or through our conservation projects around the world, to feel they can make a difference for nature.

"Our public art trails are a wonderful way to bring that belief to life."

Jersey Zoo will welcome Asiatic black bears in 2027

She said previous Go Wild Gorillas and Tortoise Takeover trails "brought so much joy to Jersey, encouraging people to explore parts of the island they might never have visited, walk new paths, meet new people and create lasting memories".

An auction of the 54 tortoise sculptures raised £720,000 for a new tropical house.

Sean and Una Brown have been together 21 years, married for 16 of them

By saving a stranger's life, Una Brown also saved her husband's.

Sean Brown was living with kidney failure and needed a transplant, but Una was not a 100% match.

The Belfast couple jumped at the chance to take part in the UK Living Kidney Sharing Scheme , external , which saw Una donate to a stranger, enabling Sean to receive a compatible organ from a different donor.

"When I was told that I wasn't a 100% match, you're automatically thinking, 'God, what's going to happen next?'

"But the fact that I could go into that sharing scheme – I had absolutely no issue with that.

"At the end of the day, if you actually think about it, two lives were saved in one day. It was the best decision of my life."

The couple with their hospital bags packed and ready to go

Sean had received his first kidney transplant aged eight – he was the face of an organ donation campaign as a child – but he always knew he might need another one in the future.

From the outset of their relationship, Una said she would give him one of hers when the time came.

"Immediately I just said - 'If you ever need a new kidney transplant, I'm going to donate' - without hesitation," she said.

Twenty-one years later, that is exactly what she did, in a roundabout way.

Sean had lived "an amazing life" for 37 years before the kidney's function started to deteriorate.

The couple entered the sharing scheme in July and the next month, Una received the news that a suitable match had been found.

"You can imagine that moment of just sheer relief," the 49-year-old council worker said.

"I genuinely cannot tell you what that felt like because it was the most emotional moment of my life.

"I knew there was hope and I knew Sean's life was going to get saved."

Sean, 45, received a call around the same time, bringing a "whirlwind of emotion".

Una wanted to reassure potential donors that it is possible to live a normal life with one kidney

The couple were initially included in a three-way transplant arrangement involving donors and recipients in different parts of the UK.

However, on the morning of surgery on 8 October, while Una was prepped for theatre, they received news that Sean's intended donor had become unwell and could no longer participate.

"I just looked at Sean and I saw his face. I thought, my God, his whole world was just crashing down around him," she said.

After an agonising wait, an alternative match emerged.

"By some miracle", Una said, the donor originally linked to her recipient was also compatible with Sean, allowing the transplant to proceed through paired donation.

Una's kidney was flown to Edinburgh, while Sean's donor kidney travelled to Belfast.

Hannah Magowan said Belfast was described as the "capital" of kidney sharing

Hannah Magowan, one of the specialist transplant surgeons at Belfast City Hospital, who performed Sean's transplant and helped with Una's surgery, said the sharing scheme had been operating in Northern Ireland since 2010.

She said it had helped almost 200 people here receive a living-donor transplant.

In 2025/26 alone, 20 of the 69 living-donor kidney transplants took place through the scheme - almost three in every 10.

Magowan said Northern Ireland had become the biggest subscribers and contributors to the scheme, despite accounting for about 3% of the UK population.

She said Belfast was described as the "capital" of kidney sharing because of the number of patients and donors coming forward.

However she added there was probably a lack of awareness about the sharing scheme as "another method of donation", even among people living with kidney disease.

Magowan said living-donor transplants could help patients avoid dialysis, as in Sean's case, and potentially lengthy waits for a deceased-donor kidney.

"It's the gift of life for someone who can't avail of a direct donation," she added. "That's sharing at its best."

Sean and Una are recovering well and intend to return to work before Christmas.

Una wanted to reassure people that she would soon be back leading a "perfectly normal" life with just one kidney.

"We're now looking to the future and if Sean gets another 37 years we'll be doing very, very well," she added.

Una said she would never know much about who received her kidney other than they were critically ill and the transplant was successful.

"You don't need to know someone to change their life," she said.

"That's the gift of life through the sharing scheme – the fact that you are making that difference."

Sean could not put into words how he felt about his wife, who had given him "the gift of life again".

He hopes their "phenomenal journey" will encourage more people to consider living donation.

Volunteers across North and South Tyneside have been pitching in to help clean the nurdles off beaches

Research into the effects of a microplastic spillage on sea-birds and marine life will be carried out for the next year after funding was secured.

A team working across Tyneside is doing tests to discover the impact the pellets, known as nurdles, have on animals, birds and fish, as well as the overall spread.

Tonnes of microplastics were spilled into the River Tyne on 19 July following a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne.

North East England Beached Bird Surveys co-ordinator Dan Turner, who is leading the research on dead sea-birds, said: "This will be a long-term issue, securing the grant now gives us room to conduct more research not just in the North East but worldwide."

Newcastle University is leading the study, which will focus on the effects of the spillage on the River Tyne and at the coast, after receiving a grant of £81,905 from the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC).

Dan Turner, from the North East Bird Survey Group, has been rinsing the stomachs of dead sea-birds

Necropsies have been carried out on dead sea-birds at the Dove Marine Laboratory in Cullercoats, North Tyneside, for the past six weeks. The current stage is focusing on stomach rinsing, which will check if nurdles have been found in the birds' stomachs.

"We haven't found any evidence of plastics in the stomachs just yet but we have more to check and have evidence that nurdles have been found in regurgitated material," Turner said.

The research was prompted over concerns birds could "starve" if they confuse the nurdles for food and fill their stomachs.

"It's concerning plastics can also break down over time which could have a big effect on the wider food chain as well," Turner added.

The research team is being led by a team of scientists and experts at Newcastle University and the University of Liverpool.

They are also being assisted by volunteers and other regional organisations such as Environment Agency, Tyne Rivers Trust and Groundwork North East and Cumbria.

Over the course of the year the research will also look to map the travel of the plastic pellets.

The nurdles have been found in beaches across Tyneside, Wearside and Teesside, with experts suggesting they may have reached the coast of Denmark.

Dr Geoffrey Abbott, a reader in geochemistry at Newcastle University, said: "We hope to visit Denmark to determine if the pellets found are the nurdles from the Port of Tyne spill.

"There have been cases where they can travel great distances, for instance a spill in South Africa led to nurdles washing up in Perth, Australia, in no time at all."

Members of the public are being asked to continue to send pictures of nurdles to help with the research.

Watch: Life in the darkness during Ukraine's blackouts

Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.

All she knows is soon the lights will go out, the sockets will lose power, the wi-fi will drop, and the taps will run dry. Tonight, the electricity has kept flowing an hour longer than advertised, but Daryna's still racing to serve dinner and finish her own work from home.

"The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."

As peace talks continue, with US envoys meeting the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.

Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn.

The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.

Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption.

"There's no light, no water, no heat, no electricity. And no fun. All the fun got sucked out with the electricity," he says. "We have a lot of board games. We have a whole shelf, but we've played them like a hundred thousand times already."

Many families sit in the shadows as blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness.

"You look outside and sometimes you see nothing. You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says.

Kyiv has been worst hit - its metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks.

We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations, barely standing after a recent ballistic missile strike - the most powerful and devastating attack of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian energy targets.

Damaged parts from the power plant lie scattered on the ground

The enormous plant - which we've been asked not to name for security reasons - has been reduced to a pile of twisted metal and broken pipes, its turbines buried in rubble, taking the site completely off line.

Volodymyr Kovalenko was on duty in the control room keeping the plant working when the missiles hit at 3am.

"It was a very powerful attack. We'd never experienced anything like it. We'd had strikes before – part of the roof had collapsed, it was pretty grim. But this time it was particularly severe."

Kovalenko, who followed in his parents' footsteps and has worked at the site for 25 years, says the damage is heartbreaking, though he's confident it can be repaired.

But the work is being hampered by air raids every 15-30 minutes – seven times during our four-hour visit. Each warning of drones and further missiles forces teams to down tools and dive for cover, though during our visit all were shot down or flew on towards other targets.

If there isn't time to reach the site's main shelter, the workers hide in the foundations of its towering chimneys.

"It's very difficult," says Vadym Bobyr, who is leading the recovery effort. "You've mentally prepared yourself to do a particular job, and then… the air raid siren goes off, and you have to get out as quickly as possible."

The 39-year-old, who has worked here half his life, is dwarfed by the mangled ruins and daunted by the challenge of rebuilding the plant.

"It's emotionally difficult, because we've already repaired all this, got it running again, and now it's happened all over again. It hurts, but we keep working and getting things done."

As we speak there's another alert - an incoming Banderol cruise missile.

The workers dart through the maze of passages and pipework but there isn't time to reach a shelter - one of the plant's thickest walls will have to do for cover. The missile was eventually intercepted 5km (3 miles) away.

The mangled wreckage of the Ukrainian power plant is still smouldering

Energy workers are at enormous risk. Since August there have been almost daily attacks on power facilities, claiming several lives every week. And it's getting more dangerous.

On the edge of the site, with the latest threat over, a team returns to reinstating the power lines feeding the national grid. But they won't be carrying electricity from the shattered plant before the end of this winter, at least.

President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine still has enough generating capacity to meet electricity demand - the problem is getting it to homes and businesses when so many power lines and substations have been hit. Russia is using "waiter drones" that cling to pylons and cables and go undetected until Russia decides to detonate them.

Maxim Timchenko, CEO of DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said Russia was already putting the degraded electricity grid under even greater pressure than last year, and that overstretched air defences were unable to protect all of Ukraine's critical infrastructure.

"What is different is the scale of attacks and the different types of weapons used in these attacks. This is what is the difference - they've doubled in power and in scale".

He said rebuilding the damaged power station would take at least until next summer, because workers under sustained attack were limited to only one or two productive hours per day.

"We are fighting for survival of not only the whole country but ordinary people, especially during winter," Timchenko says.

Volodymyr Kovalenko has worked at the power station for 25 years

Kovalenko echoes the sense of mission about trying to keep the lights on. "Energy is the foundation of everything - people's lives, the state. Nothing can function without it. I've dedicated my entire life to this".

Many are choosing to leave the capital, or Ukraine altogether, to avoid months of bitter cold. Daryna, Kyryll and Olena know the winter has barely begun.

"It's the worst feeling," Kyryll says. "When I get home from school, I'm tired. I lay in my bed. Bam! Air alarm. Bam! No lights. Bam! A lot of homework. Bam!"

When the children are in bed Daryna confides her thoughts of moving to somewhere safer, or warmer. She's torn by the desire to stay at home - close to friends and relatives - and the worry of how unbearable life may become.

The strain is damaging her mental health, she tells me, and she fears the impact on Kyryll and Olena, who suffers nightmares. Still, Daryna remains defiant despite the darkness.

"I don't want to live without light. But actually people in Ukraine say, OK, without light, but without Russians. Yes, we're scared, we're scared a lot. But better for us to be without power, but [also] without Russians."

Watch: Aerial video shows survivor being pulled from collapsed building in New York

Several people have died after a New York City building containing apartments collapsed into a neighbouring open construction site on Wednesday afternoon.

More than a dozen others are injured, and some of them are in a critical condition, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News, which cited local officials.

The collapse sparked a massive search-and-rescue operation, with more than 250 first responders going to the scene of the fallen three-storey building in Brooklyn.

Aerial footage has shown firefighters pulling a survivor, covered in dust, out of the debris on a stretcher. She was later said to have been a pregnant woman.

Officials previously said they did not know how many others are missing. The BBC has contacted the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) for further comment.

An investigation is under way into what caused the sudden collapse.

Witnesses described a terrifying sound as the building came down at about 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT).

"I live literally right behind the building," one woman, Emmanuella Carilus, told the New York Times. "It sounded like a big boom and you just heard a bunch of screaming."

The newspaper published images showing a crowd of fire trucks and police vehicles at the same, and wrote that the noise of sirens had not stopped in the area.

"I've never seen anything like this," said another witness, named only as Dashik, who spoke to local television station PIX 11.

Officials are yet to identify those who died or were injured.

Officials say the rescue efforts could last for days

Locals have gathered at the scene to await news of those feared to have been caught in the collapse.

The rescue mission has been described as "extremely dangerous" by New York City Fire Department (FDNY) Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore.

She added that people from the collapsed building and also the construction site had been trapped.

"Members have been working methodically and haven't stopped since they arrived this afternoon," Bonsignore said.

The woman who was filmed being rescued from the rubble was identified by her husband.

Speaking to a reporter from CBS News New York, he described his relief after an anxious wait: "She is alive. She is still alive. I'm very happy. I'm very happy. I'm very happy. I thank all of you guys. She's pregnant, six months."

Rescuers have used search dogs, drones, axes and chainsaws to carry out their work. They say they anticipate the effort will last for several days.

The collapse exposed parts of the building's interior as emergency services worked at the scene on Thursday

Some pictures of the collapsed building, on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn, show an entire side of it gone, with bedrooms and closets exposed. Among the debris, smashed concrete and twisted metal, are household items and clothes.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined emergency responders at the scene, praising them for their rapid response.

They "arrived in under a minute and have spent hours working in dangerous and highly technical conditions to rescue New Yorkers," he later wrote on X.

The Brooklyn building was built in 1930, city records show, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.

At the adjacent construction site, where plans have been approved for a new building, active work was going on when the incident occurred, according to FDNY Chief of Department John Esposito.

The activity was described by another official as "excavation work". It was not immediately clear whether the work had anything to do with the collapse of the neighbouring building.

James has won 68 caps for Wales since making his debut eight years ago

Winger Dan James says Wales proved a point when they beat Norway – but is wary Erling Haaland and his team-mates are now intent on turning the tables.

The Leeds United attacker said that Craig Bellamy's side were being written off before the eye-catching win in Cardiff last month.

James was on the scoresheet as Wales came from behind to see off the World Cup quarter-finalists, reigniting hopes of staying in the top tier of the Nations League.

It represented the biggest scalp of Bellamy's reign, ending a winless run of six and quietening some of the rumblings of discontent around the manager.

Repeating the trick in Oslo on Saturday (17:00 GMT) would inch Wales to within a whisker of securing third spot and the boost to Euro 2028 qualifying seedings that comes with it.

In contrast, Norway are on their worst run of form in a decade and in danger of dropping out of the European elite they seemed on course to challenge.

"They're a great nation and, at home especially, they've been brilliant," said James as Wales prepared for the encounter at Ullevaal Stadion.

"They're a very hard team to beat and I think after having that win in Cardiff it's something that they've had to take – and they'll be even more up for this game."

Wales boss Bellamy praises Liverpool's handling of Koumas

Johnson says definitely more to come after 50 caps

Norwegian media were critical of the side that lost in Cardiff having also been beaten in games against Portugal immediately before and after.

The defeat in Oslo – in which Cristiano Ronaldo was left on the bench by Portugal, prompting his walk out and eventual international retirement – was the first time Norway had lost in 12 competitive matches at home.

And Norway have not lost four games in a row since 2016, well before the emergence of much of their current golden generation.

Only veteran goalkeeper Orjan Nyland and fit-again Atletico Madrid striker Alexander Sorloth survive from that time.

It suggests Wales will face a side eager to end talk of such issues with a win this weekend.

James, though, says Wales will be focusing on themselves after silencing critics against the same opposition.

"We won't look to them too much - they've got great players, they've got a great squad and have been great at home – but we have full belief," said the 29-year-old set to win his 69th cap.

"That win over Norway was so important to keep us in the group and we showed what we were about."

Wales had been under fire after losing their opening League A fixtures in Portugal and Denmark, the latter seeing head coach Bellamy admit he had been "hurt" by the performance.

"The manager said it and we all knew it - we didn't perform to our best," James added.

"As a team, we lost our identity a little bit. People had started talking and writing us off a little bit, but I think we showed our reaction and people saw."

Dan James scored in Wales' 2-1 victory over Norway in October

A win in Oslo would leave Wales handily placed to seal at least third in the group, providing they could then either pick up a point in Cardiff against Portugal in their final fixture or hope results go their way.

Although it would likely mean Wales would still have to go to a play-off to retain their League A status, it would guarantee a pot one seeding for the Euro 2028 qualifiers – a tournament Wales will co-host.

"We're all aware of where we want to finish and how important it is going into Euro qualifiers," said James, who was part of the Wales squads that appeared at Euro 2020 and the 2022 World Cup – the nation's last major final appearances.

"We have it in the back of our heads, but we can't put pressure on ourselves – the only thing to know is that if we perform, we can do it.

"We know we have two very important games against teams we want to be playing against. If we want to get to major finals and go far in tournaments, we have to be able to compete against these teams and the manager always reiterates that."
