The government is prepared to force the entertainment industry to improve safeguarding practices unless rapid change is introduced, BBC Newsnight has learned.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told the House of Commons she will meet representatives from the media, entertainment and sport next week to "discuss the action that we need to take" following recent allegations.

"But if those protections are insufficient, the government will not hesitate to take further action," she said.

She could force participation in creative industries industry standards body CIISA, which is currently voluntary, to protect whistleblowers, the BBC understands.

Her comments come after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that entertainer David Walliams had been accused by several women of sexual misconduct and abusing his position, which he denies.

Nandy added: "For too long, too many people have had to choose between their career and their safety.

"Whistleblowers must be protected, and those who abuse their position must no longer be able to hide."

Earlier this week, she said she was summoning leaders from the broadcasting, publishing, film and entertainment industries to "draw a line" in the sand.

That announcement came after the publication of allegations against Walliams, as well as the sentencing of disgraced entertainer Russell Brand on charges of rape and sexual assault.

The allegations against Walliams were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation that was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public. Walliams denies all the allegations against him.

BBC Newsnight understands that the culture secretary will deliver two messages at next week's round-table meeting.

In the first instance, she will tell industry leaders that they need to meet the moment, take responsibility and tackle issues of safeguarding on their own. But she will add that if their response is not good enough, the government might have to intervene.

Intervention could include forcing participation in the CIISA.

The culture secretary also said she recently appointed two "freelance champions in recognition of the fact that for freelancers in particular, there is a real problem in these industries."

Multiple government ministers gave statements on Wednesday that called for further restrictions on the use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).

Women and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson told Sky News that there was "scope to go further" on legislation that restricted the use of such agreements to ensure that the legal system was not being "abused in order to silence women".

"We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals - rich and powerful men - are able to silence women and stop things coming to light," she said.

Zelda Perkins, who spoke out against Harvey Weinstein, tells Newsnight of NDA challenges

Can't Buy My Silence founder Zelda Perkins told BBC Newsnight that there were "not enough safeguards" around high-profile people in creative industries and that joining the CIISA should be "mandatory".

The former assistant to jailed film producer Harvey Weinstein broke an NDA in 2017 when she spoke publicly about the movie mogul's mistreatment of women.

She has since founded a group that campaigns against NDAs being used in legal contracts or settlements to stop people from speaking out against their employers.

"There are no other regulatory bodies that are voluntary to join," Perkins told BBC Newsnight, referring to CIISA, noting that "obviously the people who need to be monitored are the people who are not joining".

"It's still very wild west in the the creative industries, people behave how they want," she said, adding that while "you can't change the humans, you can change the rules around them".

David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct after losing injunction bid

Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand

In the initial investigation published by the Guardian, some of the women accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line .

Separately, a producer who worked on a TV show on which Walliams was a celebrity guest several years ago has told the BBC she was instructed to keep the comedian away from young female members of staff.

Speaking anonymously, she said she was warned that Walliams was "creepy" and "inappropriate", and that it was "well-known" he should not be put with young female runners.

She said she "wasn't at all surprised" when allegations about Walliams' behaviour emerged.

The Guardian reported that lawyers representing Walliams said he had never been warned nor "got into trouble" for messaging runners, and that he denied he behaved inappropriately and harassed young women in the workplace.

Comedian Kate Smurthwaite told BBC Newsnight that Walliams was a name that came up "over and over again", and that there was a "sense of worry" about him working with young people.

Watch: Comedian Kate Smurthwaite shares comments made over Walliams' alleged behaviour

"People were saying that they knew people who had worked with him and either felt very uncomfortable and left, or stuck around and felt that his behaviour was inappropriate," she said.

When asked why it had taken so long for such allegations to emerge, Smurthwaite said: "We all know that women who raise these issues, there's a backlash, which might be legal, it might be in terms of your career or your opportunities, it might be as subtle as being seen as a problem."

Surgeon films damage in Nasser hospital in Gaza

Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.

The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".

The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.

Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".

Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.

Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.

Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.

Pictures showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics

The Nasser Medical Complex is located in the city of Khan Younis and is the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serving almost one million people.

In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said a missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.

Other footage shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by an explosion.

The hospital's director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, later told a news conference that Israeli forces had fired two missiles at the al-Yasin surgery building but that only one exploded.

"What's happened in Nasser Medical Complex is targeting the health sector mainly. We are talking about doctors, we are talking about civilians, we are talking about patients," he said.

"Also, there is... huge damage [to] the infrastructure inside the hospital."

Footage filmed by a freelance journalist working for the BBC showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics, as well as hallways and lifts.

News agencies also published photos that appeared to show an unexploded missile.

Photographs appeared to show an unexploded missile inside Nasser hospital's surgical building

Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgery specialist who was wounded in the head, said he and other medical staff had just finished work around 00:30 and had been preparing to go to sleep when there was an explosion.

"My whole body was trapped under the rubble. For a moment, I felt as if I was about to lose consciousness, or that I was about to die," he told the BBC.

"I started struggling to free myself and started calling out, 'Guys! Guys!' I began crawling, trying to pull my leg out from beneath the rubble. I managed to pull myself free. It was dark, there were no lights, nothing at all."

He said he had been lying in a bed near Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, who was killed. Another colleague suffered a broken leg.

"Dr Rizq was the kindest person in this department. He was very kind and always willing to help... And of course, he was a surgeon, one of the best among us."

He added: "Patients were killed as well. There were patients in the rooms next to us who were killed. A patient comes to the hospital seeking treatment and leaves carried on people's shoulders. I do not know what kind of humanity this is."

Gaza's health ministry said surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira was among those killed

The Israeli military said in a statement that its "precise strike" had targeted the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, who it named as Mohammed Abu Ismail, alongside other fighters who were "hiding inside" Nasser hospital.

"The terrorists were struck in order to remove the threat they posed after turning the Nasser hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there to advance dozens of terrorist plots against our forces and restore the brigade's force," it alleged.

The military added that it had issued advance warnings before the strike and released an audio recording of what it said was one given to a senior Gaza health official. But Fara insisted the hospital had received no warning of an attack.

A Hamas statement rejected the Israeli military's accusations, calling them "a blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility whose function and purpose are well known".

"The nature of the targeted site and the casualties inflicted on patients, doctors and medical staff expose the falsity and weakness of this narrative," it said.

However, local activists circulated claims overnight that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.

Fara said this was the seventh time that Nasser hospital had been struck during the war. In August 2025, a double Israeli strike killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said it had documented a total of 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths.

"Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," warned Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the UN agency's director general.

Later on Thursday, at least four more Palestinians were reportedly killed in separate incidents in northern and central Gaza.

Medics said three were killed in Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, Jabalia and Deir al-Balah, while the fourth was killed by Israeli gunfire in Bureij refugee camp.

The Israeli military said it struck a "terrorist" in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City.

Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October last year.

More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza also remains dire and has recently deteriorated further as a result of heavy rains last weekend that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Moment teen rescued after six days in Australian bush

A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.

William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.

Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.

He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".

Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.

The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.

"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.

"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."

Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."

Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.

"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

Councils across England own hundreds of thousands artworks, but what are they doing with it all?

Fewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found.

More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage.

Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK.

Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art.

Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley.

Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council.

Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds.

As of April, just 26,899 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have?

Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display.

All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April.

Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities.

"If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said.

"It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think."

Sally Godden said the museum team aimed to ensure the council collection instilled "pride in the people of Rugby"

Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset.

"We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people."

The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection.

Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years.

Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24.

The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of.

For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools.

When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection.

Rugby, which is among the councils adding to their collections, recently acquired a painting selected by students and pupils living in the town

Kent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April.

At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept.

"I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so."

The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North.

The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives".

Art UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks , external .

Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art.

"We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place.

"The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time.

"From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it."

He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances.

Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits.

But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums".

Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26.

Keeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work.

Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display.

One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum .

Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works.

Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public.

That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events.

It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation.

Mark Doyle said it was "fair to say that when we reopen, there will be more of the collections on display at any one time than there ever has been"

Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme.

"We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on."

Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council.

"A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said.

Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time.

"Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment."
